speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, January 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and on the amendment of Mr. Gray (Windsor West) (p. 1302).

Mr. Speaker, I want to continue my remarks with regard to the amendment and the Bill known as Investment Canada which is before the House. When this Bill was introduced I was somewhat concerned that it came at an inopportune time. I thought, as did many Canadians, that due to the statements made in the Throne Speech and the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and more particularly the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), that a great deal of consultation would take place in Canada with regard to legislation and the direction in which they wished to take the Government of Canada.
Unfortunately, the opposite is the case. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) really wants to be the Minister of Finance, as evidenced by his actions. The Minister of Finance talks of consultation on one hand, but on the other hand implements action without any consultation. I find it quite disturbing that there was no consultation on an important piece of legislation like Investment Canada. The provinces of Canada were not consulted.
All through the years that the Conservative Party was in opposition, and particularly in the pre-election days, the sentiment was expressed that provincial Governments across the country ought to be consulted on a regular basis, not only with regard to the process but with regard to the substance. Again, Mr. Speaker, there was no consultation whatsoever. I thought that perhaps the Conservative Government would have placed the issue of foreign investment on the agenda as an item to be discussed at the economic summit. Again we hear the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance talk of consultation, mutterings if you will, and then they do the exact opposite,
which is unilaterally to bring in a piece of legislation which Canadians wish to be consulted upon.
There is a need in this country for consultation about foreign investment and foreign control because it affects the daily lives of Canadians across the country. Foreign investment is an important issue. I do not have to remind Members of all the industries that are foreign controlled in Canada, but I think it would be appropriate to list three or four. The tobacco industry is 99 per cent foreign controlled. The rubber products industry is 90 per cent foreign controlled. There is 75 per cent foreign control in the chemical industry and 70 per cent foreign control of transportation fuels. There are some very important industries in Canada that are foreign controlled and I am certain that Canadians, at least in my constituency, would like to have been consulted about those changes which the Government has brought in.
I take issue with some of the comments and statements made by members of the Conservative Party that the previous Foreign Investment Review Act was hindering foreign investment in Canada. The facts do not bear that up. The fact is that over 90 per cent of those applications which were submitted and processed were approved. That is a pretty good batting average in any game. I believe that it is not very logical to suggest that the fact that a small number of applicants have been refused or the process was slowed is reason to throw out the Foreign Investment Review Act. However, it is very valid to say that where the process was slow it ought to have been improved. We attempted to do that in 1982.
I think we have lessened the negative impact or criticisms made by individuals with regard to the Foreign Investment Review Act. I do not wish to suggest that the Foreign Investment Review Act was perfect because it was not. However, I wish to quote what Duncan McDowall said about the Foreign Investment Review Agency in Canada. He talked about Canada as a place for investment and said: "Canada has long been considered a stable and remunerative place for foreign investment".
The points which are trying to be raised by the Conservative Government are simply not valid. Canada is a good place for foreign investment and we had a very good regime in Canada to protect and enhance that foreign investment in order that we may create jobs.
Other countries like Canada have had apparatus put in place to guard against foreign investment. We need look no further than the United States to see such things as shipping, broadcasting and air transportation which have restrictions with regard to foreign investment. I point out to the House

Investment Canada Act
that Australia also has a regime for foreign investment. Japan also has a regime to guard against and promote, if you will, foreign investment in that country. Therefore Canada had a good regime with the Foreign Investment Review Act. It has been displaced by Investment Canada. I must say that this has been done through the back door in the sense that the Government has predicated the Investment Canada Act on the claim that it will create thousands upon thousands of new jobs.
I have asked the Minister and members of the Conservative Government to show the documented evidence which would prove unequivocally that thousands upon thousands of new jobs would be created by more foreign investment and by relaxing the standards that were already in place. Where is the evidence? There is no evidence. It is a smoke and mirrors situation put in place by the Prime Minister.
As we all know, the Prime Minister is kowtowing to the Americans at every opportunity. I believe this is threatening our sovereignty as a nation. I do not want Canada to become the next state of the United States; I want Canada to continue as an independent country both in terms of its foreign policy and in terms of investment and economic policy. It is utter nonsense to think that Canadians will believe that thousands of new jobs will be created with the introduction of Investment Canada. The same myth was perpetrated against the Canadian people during the election. The Prime Minister said: "Elect me and tens of thousands of new jobs will be created". That has not been the case. He said that overnight these jobs would be created, but that has not been the case, Mr. Speaker.

What about Investment Canada? How many jobs will come out of this? Will it be one million jobs in four years or 1.3 million? What will it be? This type of thing shows a lack of depth by the Conservative Party, in particular by the Prime Minister and the sheep who sit behind him. I say to you in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that this Tory Government bent on selling Canada to the United States will have a great fall in the next general election.

Mr. Speaker, in the view of the majority of Canadians the most serious problem facing this country is the tremendous number of unemployed. There are 1.5 million people unemployed. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) recognized that this was the main problem. During the election campaign he said the major issue that he wanted to address was jobs, jobs, jobs.
The Bill we have before us now is supposed to help us achieve the objective of job creation, according to the Government. The Government is arguing that if we only throw open the doors to more foreign investment and remove the very minimally slow downs created by the Foreign Investment Review Agency, the money will flow into Canada and create jobs.
Newspapers such as The Globe and Mail and The Financial Times have analysed this question and made it very clear, as a result of discussions with American investors, that there will
be no quick movement of investment capital into Canada as a result of the passage of this Bill.
This Government seems to believe that any investment is good investment. With very few exceptions the Government intends to open the doors and put this country on the sales block. Everything will go to the highest bidder.
In the few minutes I have I would like to deal with just one aspect of investment that leads to job creation, namely the critical ingredient of research and development. The Government has emphasized the importance of research and development, particularly in the dynamic sectors of electronics, manufacturing, telecommunications, software development and other high-tech areas. The fact is that among all the industrialized countries Canada is virtually at the bottom in terms of the percentage of our Gross National Product which is allocated to research and development. While we are still hovering at about a 1.5 per cent allocation of our GNP to research and development, many of other countries are now investing 2.5 per cent or more of their Gross National Product in research and development. They are forging ahead of us, Mr. Speaker, in the use of the newest technologies.
We are told to let the money come into Canada and there will be more jobs. But in the manufacturing sector where over 50 per cent of the enterprises are already foreign owned, we have virtually no interest in, no expenditure and no concentration on, research and development. I will come back to that if I have time.
We have found, and studies have made it clear, that major efforts in the field of research and development in Canada are carried out and have been for a number of years either in Canadian universities, Government departments or Crown corporations, such as the National Research Council. These bodies are the ones which have done the research and they are now suffering from the Government's unwillingness to play a major role in stimulating research and development activities because funds have either been frozen or, even worse, cut by the Government.
I want to give one specific illustration of what I mean, Mr. Speaker. There is no better signal of the Government's contradictory strategy than the move that has been taken to eliminate the Institute of Manufacturing Technology in my home city of Winnipeg. Winnipeg is a manufacturing centre in its own right. Also it is home to two major universities and several technical institutions. It was logical to choose Winnipeg as the home of this centre which had as an objective the kind of research and development work not now being done in this country-the revitalization of techniques, processes and methods which could be used in manufacturing in the country or marketed abroad as applications in other countries.
IMT was located in Winnipeg not as a result of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) pushing the idea while he was a Cabinet Minister. It was not an example of porkbarrel politics. It was the result of long-term planning by the Manitoba Research Council which dealt with

a proposal by the then Conservative Government of Manitoba to the National Research Council in 1980. An enormous amount of planning went into IMT only to be scuttled by the Government which now intends to open the doors to the free and unfettered exportation of American jobs.
The intention was to tie in the academic resources of the Universities of Winnipeg and Manitoba, the research facilities of the National Research Council and the expertise and industry experience of the private manufacturing and production sector. This is the kind of labour-intensive activity which creates beneficial spin-offs. Already 42 of the anticipated 125-member staff of the institute have been hired. Major equipment has been ordered and received. Research projects have begun at various locations across the country. To eliminate this project now is the worst of mistakes and completely contrary to this Government's supposed policy.
It was at IMT that Canada was to begin to address the problems of adapting technology, developing new processes in such advanced areas as flexible manufacturing systems, sensors, robotics, computer-aided design and manufacturing, and artificial intelligence. All these areas offer great promise and are being investigated in other countries. All could aid in giving this country the advanced manufacturing capability it needs. Yet one of the first steps taken by the Government was to cancel a project into which so much effort had been put, a project which would have benefited not only my City of Winnipeg but manufacturing facilities all across the country.
As I said earlier, many people work in the manufacturing industries. More than half of this sector is U.S. controlled and very little research and development is being done by it. One of the largest corporations in Canada is General Motors. It is virtually doing no research in automobiles in this country. Not only is it conducting research in automobiles in the United States, but it is now branching into other important fields in that country.
I should like to refer to an article which appeared some time ago in The New York Times. It indicated that the General Motors Corporation was beginning a major new research effort to integrate computers, software, robots, sensors and telecommunications systems into a highly automated manufacturing process that might lower the cost of producing automobiles and conceivably revolutionize production processes in a range of other industries. Similarly, a major chemical company in Canada, du Pont, is embarking upon new research efforts, not in Canada but in the United States. The New York Times reported that du Pont was embarking upon research to penetrate the life sciences, biotechnological and electronic areas. Scientists at du Pont are studying such varied subjects as the structures of polymer chemicals, the genetic controls of tobacco plants, the molecular biology of immunology and leukemia, and optical laser recording disks, all in this in the U.S.A.
Are they proposing to do anything in Canada? Not at all. We have the beginnings of very interesting and competitive micro-electronic companies and the beginnings of companies involved in biotechnology. These are small companies but they

can lead to whole new industries which employ many people. They are cash poor and are logical candidates for a takeover by American companies. When these companies are taken over, the jobs that have been developed will be moved to the United States.
For that reason among others, I and the members of my Party oppose this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in this debate on the amendment to Bill C-15, as proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray).

This Bill has been debated in this House for a number of days. It is becoming more and more evident that the people of this country do not want this type of legislation. If government Members across the way and those who are commonly referred to as the book-ends, those who sit on the opposite side of the Chamber from the rest of their colleagues, would take a few moments to do the following exercise, it would be of great benefit to them and their constituents.
Over the next few weeks I intend to consult the people of my riding on this issue. My next constituency mail-out will contain a questionnaire. I will ask the people of the great riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell how they feel about Bill C-15 and its potential effect of reducing Canadian ownership of our industries. From discussions I have had with the people in my riding I am sure that neither they nor the rest of the people of Canada favour this type of Bill.
When I was a member of the Ontario legislature, I sent out a questionnaire which included a similar question. The question was: "Do you feel that there is a sufficient amount of Canadian ownership of our industry at the present time?". Another question was: "Are you in favour of stricter measures to ensure that Canadian ownership of our industries is maintained?". The large majority of voters in my riding consistently expressed the view that we do not have enough control over our industries at the present time and that we should not allow the situation to deteriorate further.
The intent of this Bill is puzzling. The Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) described how this Bill leads us to believe that it proposes freer restrictions and wide open policies that we will be advertising in the United States and has certain hidden restrictions which, although not immediately apparent, are there. This schizophrenic feature of the Bill is somewhat confusing.
Let me give a few examples of how this Bill is confusing. We are told there will be exemption of all new business investment and all direct investments involving assets under $5 million. How does one determine whether the assets of a particular company are under $5 million? The only way to do that is to have the new agency review all pertinent documents, the books and so forth of that company, as was done in the past. Once

Investment Canada Act
those companies are reviewed, we can tell them that we do not have to review them because they have less than the amount that was advocated by the new Bill. Of course, in order to find that out, we must go through the process.
I find that particular feature of the new Bill to be somewhat confusing. Perhaps government Members would seize the opportunity afforded to them by the speech rotation to explain to us specifically how one would be able to identify whether or not new companies qualify under this Bill for the reasons I have previously mentioned without going through the process of examining their books. It seems to me that that is inconsistent with what the Government is attempting to do.
We are told that the final authority is now to be vested with the Minister rather than the Cabinet and that no provision for appeal to a higher authority is formally stated. Again that is a rather confusing position on the part of government Members, who on the one hand attempt to attribute to themselves such adjectives as free, open and democratic, and on the other hand will now give power to one Minister rather than giving it to the entire Cabinet, which in my view is a more democratic way of doing things. Again this is inconsistent with the message government Members are attempting to send to Americans and to all foreign investors.
We have also heard that the criterion for permitting acquisition has changed from "significant" to "net" benefit. Whether one word is used or another, it is quite obvious that we will have to examine such benefit as is derived from an investor before being able to determine whether the benefit is significant or only net.
Regardless, I think it is obvious that a good part of the process which existed before will be retained even though government Members are attempting to say the opposite. Nevertheless, the clear message they are sending is that the previous legislation was ineffective and did not welcome foreign investment. If that was the case, then why was it, as pointed out by the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), that the approval rate was 97 per cent? If foreign investment was not welcome, why did we approve 97 per cent of it? Presumably, Mr. Speaker, we did so because the previous legislation was indeed quite effective.
I think it is important to recognize that at one point the previous legislation needed amending and it was amended to reflect changing times. It is true that foreign investment is welcome. However, it is not true to say, as government Members are attempting to say to the Americans, that foreign investment shall be unrestrained.
We respect the United States. It is our very close neighbour, a very powerful nation in the world and a nation which has been very friendly to us. However, as I said when I spoke on this issue previously, just because someone is our friend does not mean that we open our door, give him a set of keys and let him in at any time. I have friends but I do not give them keys to my house. If I do, I do it sparingly and for very good reasons. However, doing that does not make our friends any
less friendly to us. It simply means that we assert the authority that we have as a nation. I do think it is time that we recognized that to be masters of our own house does not mean that we are to be unfriendly.
Some of my colleagues have stated that the United States and indeed several other countries do have restrictions like we have and some countries are even stricter than us with regard to the ownership of airlines, broadcast industries and so on. Recognizing that and recognizing that other countries surely have a right to such restrictions, we must recognize that we have a right to such restrictions as well.
I am thinking of the situation which now exists in this country with regard to restrictions planned for the area of agriculture. I am sure all Hon. Members of the House are familiar with the potential danger created by the Americans cutting off imports of pork products from Canada to the United States. Several thousands of jobs could potentially be affected by this. We do not hear that discussed much in the House. The only think we hear from the Government is that we should have our door wide open. When we greet a friend we sometimes do open the door, but we must recognize that we are our own masters and that foreign investment in this country, albeit welcome, should only be allowed when it is of the greatest benefit to all Canadians.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I would like to offer you and all Members of this House my best wishes for the new year, and I hope that what we do this year will be of benefit to all Canadians.
I represent the riding of Beauce, where Canada begins. We are on the U.S. border, with the State of Maine as our neighbour. As you may know, the people of Beauce tend to get along very well with their neighbours and to co-operate with them, so we are particularly aware of the benefits of good relations, and I am therefore on familiar ground when I speak to Bill C-15.
Canada's national policy must be based on international objectives. Economic renewal starts with renewed investment, a very welcome challenge for this Government. The people who elected us have faith in us. We must keep a level head and we must be realistic. We all want to succeed, but we will have to open our doors to investors, to those whose faith in our country and our government has been restored. Investment capital remains the basis for economic success.
Investment is the key to economic growth because it will help finance the facilities that will make Canada more productive and create more jobs for Canadians. That is what we want. Canadians will appreciate this new boost for the economy, because the unemployment rate in Canada is now 11 per cent, while the real rate is probably even higher. Considering this situation, Mr. Speaker, we must ask ourselves what FIRA has been able to achieve after ten years of operations and

whether it has any legitimacy. That is why our Government has decided to act by tabling this very important piece of legislation. We must remember that before the good years in the sixties and early seventies, Canada was built on foreign investment, first British and then mainly American, and that without such investment, it would have been impossible to industrialize this country.
Whenever measures to control foreign investment were introduced as an expression of nationalistic fervour, they have led to underdevelopment, and I am thinking, for instance, of Argentina and Mexico. Local capital has never benefited from such measures, since it is a fact that the specific nature of investment, a critical factor in industry, is to act as an engine, not as a dead weight. Our economic growth depends on investment. In Canada, a good example would be the oil industry. Sheltered like a hothouse plant by the Liberals' National Energy Program, Canada's oil industry has lost access to foreign capital, resulting in the unprecedented action taken by the Government, and I would refer Hon. Members to the monster Petro-Canada has become.
According to Jacques Forget, editorial writer for "Finance" in Montreal, in addition to investment being the economy's moving force, its impact is reinforced by what economists refer to as the multiplier effect. Traditionally, foreign investment in Canada has been the prime engine of economic development. A responsible government, as we claim to be, must act to bring down a federal deficit that has increased steadily under the Liberals.
This Government realizes that to encourage economic growth in this country, it will have to gag FIRA. After the Prime Minister's speech before the Economic Club in New York recently, foreign investors realized that with the advent of the Progressive Conservatives, Canada would again become a prime investment area, where investors would be able to invest safely and profitably. We are going to show our confidence in the long-term investors, in business and in the individual entrepreneur. The Canadian economy will benefit as a result of increased employment and a rising balance of payments, a decisive factor in determining the value of the dollar, all of which will certainly reduce pressure on interest rates.
All this can be done because this Government is a Government of people who work, people who save, people who invest, people who create businesses and jobs. Mr. Speaker, there is a renewed faith in the free market system, in the freedom of Canadians and in Canada.
For 20 years we have been living beyond our means because of an irresponsible Government, some of whose members are among the survivors opposite, now under a new leader with a recycled image. Since September 4, Canadians have had confidence in our Government and according to the polls they are showing that confidence today. It is a Government that is promoting realistic and courageous policies.

Mr. Speaker, on the Opposition side we often hear a number of fantastic and I might even say frivolous comments. Why don't these people stand up to make speeches and give their point of view? All we hear are a lot of grunts and groans that tend to disturb whoever has the floor. We must make difficult choices for the benefit of future generations. Canadians put an end to Liberal rhetoric when they realized that Liberal Government was not the solution to Canada's problems because it was the problem.
Future capital requirements will probably exceed any since the industrial boom right after the Second World War. Expanding industries such as telecommunications, robotics, computer systems and genetic engineering all require massive investment and are thus capital-based. For instance, today's secretary works on equipment worth $3,000, but tomorrow's secretary who will be a computer specialist, will require an investment of as much as $25,000. The growth in productivity will certainly be considerable-that is not the point. When all is said and done, we have no choice. Increasingly, our labour force will consist mainly of people who are qualified for white-collar jobs. They will not be productive unless they have the tools this kind of work requires and unless we can benefit from adequate foreign investment.
Mr. Speaker, let us be realistic. We must understand and accept that any reduction in youth unemployment will have to be preceded by foreign investment. Those who are opposed to foreign investment are thereby opposed to reintegrating young people in the labour market. We must realize that we will not get the jobs Canadians need unless we invest the capital this requires. We must be realistic. We need others to help our economy grow. President Reagan has understood this. The economic upsurge in the United States is mainly due to an increase in investment which means greater confidence in the government. This has helped increase GNP growth from 0.7 to 1.8 points, thanks to the pro-business philosophy of the Reagan Administration.
Mr. Speaker, if the United States is able to attract foreign capital, why should Canada not attract capital from the United States and elsewhere? Our country has to rebuild capital supplies to meet the challenge of a new industrial revolution. This month, in his message on the State of the Union, President Reagan stated, and I shall end on this note: "America is back". We might add: "Canada will follow".

Mr. Speaker, I rise to join in the debate on Bill C-15, the Investment Canada Bill, and I speak in support of the amendment before the House to read the Bill a second time six months hence.
I am opposed to any relaxation of a law which already allows decisions to be made regarding investments that are against national interests and will increase the possibility that such development of the Canadian economy will not serve the needs of Canadians, whether as Canadian investors, as engi-

neers and developers of technology, or as suppliers of products. On a number of different points it is possible to demonstrate not that we need a relaxation of the law, but that instead we should administer more strongly the legislation which already exists.
1 would like to explore some of these areas because it is very important to appreciate what will be the consequences of these decisions. In the process of thinking about these decisions we must ask ourselves whether the Government has done more than to suggest in an ideological way, as an article of faith-as did the last speaker-that we need to open the doors wide, and that it is only by those means that we can ensure that the country will achieve full employment and that Canadians will again know prosperity.
The Foreign Investment Review Agency has been in operation for about a decade. The record of the Agency demonstrates the importance of political will. In particular, during 1984 it became obvious that a Government that was not concerned about the consequences of foreign investment- which was recognized time and again at the end of the 1960s and through the 1970s-could in fact ensure that the Foreign Investment Review Agency represented little hindrance to foreign investment. One could conclude from that that the legislation before us is to some extent designed to fly the flag, or perhaps to pull the flag down, before foreign investors, in a supine surrender to their investment decisions which would be exercised in Canada.
During 1984 FIRA approved many foreign investment decisions. In only a very small number of those cases did it actually require foreign investment to lead to the creation of employment in Canada. In few of the cases did it even require that there be new investment in Canada from outside. From the beginning of 1984, 16 per cent of the applications approved promised neither new jobs nor new investment. Of course, in those cases one had to ask what were the consequences of the investment decisions being approved, considering the change of control which was taking place in Canada with the foreign operators having a larger influence in the direction of the Canadian economy. On that point I could say that the consequences of these foreign investment decisions have become quite clear in my own community.

In the last week there has been concern in the City of Thunder Bay about the prospect that one of the stores which Canada Safeway operates is likely to be lost. During 1983 the food retailing business in Thunder Bay was significantly consolidated when Loblaws and Dominion Stores retired from the scene. The A & P and Canada Safeway took over these stores and established, as far as national retailing outlets are concerned, a "duopoly" in which the two of them were jostling for control of the market. The Foreign Investment Review Agency allowed that to go ahead even though it realized that Canada Safeway, in its acquisitions in Thunder Bay, Winnipeg, Regina and perhaps other centres, was significantly increasing its domination of the market. What FIRA apparently did was to
require some reduction of outlets as a means of trying to increase competition and reduce this domination.
It now seems that Canada Safeway has been using that decision as a means of closing down perhaps its oldest and smallest outlets in order to consolidate its operations in large centres. What this means for one area of Thunder Bay is the loss of an old and much patronized store, forcing its patrons to go some distance to shop. In the case of senior citizens who do not have cars this would mean travelling by bus or probably by taxi in making trips of some distance in order to buy their groceries. That is obviously a serious matter for people with very limited incomes.
Of course, blaming this on FIRA is taking the matter up in mid-course. What we have to consider far more is the activities of large food retailers, in this case two American-controlled companies, who have succeeded in establishing dominance in a community and then forcing people into that kind of unfortunate plight. Obviously one can only regret the disappearance of Dominion and Loblaws from Thunder Bay because they represented more competition in the market. Surely this is a demonstration of what the consequences of foreign investment can be.
I submit that we have not had any substantial demonstration in this country of the advantages of foreign investment. People say as an article of faith that it is necessary, but of course my colleagues have taken a leading part in focusing on the dangerous consequences. We have had a great deal of superficial discussion of foreign investment. However, there has been little recognition of the fact that the kind of foreign investment we are faced with these days is one particular style of putting capital to work which has much more far-reaching consequence than some of the other possibilities.
When this matter was being debated last December, someone asked about the extent of British investment in the United States through the 19th century. What that person failed to note is that that investment was very largely that of portfolio investment. That is to say, British investors bought shares in companies. They invested in American railway bonds or whatever. Unless they were brought together in a committee because the enterprise was not doing well, they were hardly involved in any kind of controlling interest in the activity.
Portfolio investment, joint ventures and possibly licensing agreements are all means by which capital can be obtained. But what is not being recognized by our colleagues on the government benches for the danger it represents to the Canadian economy is that foreign investment these days is in the form of a subsidiary. No matter how profitable it is, a closely held corporation will never be available for investment by Canadians unless we have a tightening of the law and we demand that the enterprise offer shares to Canadians so they can participate in the profits. Instead we have a subsidiary with presumably some injection of foreign capital at the outset, but after that it draws on Canadian capital sources. That surely, even on the theory our friends have on the other side, will represent a reduction in capital available to Canadians.

In these various ways, where the subsidiary draws on foreign technology rather than encouraging Canadian technology and research and development, where it draws on the parent for products and encourages the importation of materials to Canada rather than production in Canada, we then see the way in which the activities of the subsidiary go against the national economic interest. In those circumstances I can only regret on behalf of the Canadian people that a government which calls itself national will undertake these actions of expressing a colonial mentality in selling out the interests of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, in the eighties, few people fail to agree with the need to increase investment capital, both foreign and domestic, in order to give our economic development a new impulse. Clearly FIRA, which approved more than 90 per cent of foreign investment applications over the last ten years, has played a major role in developing our economy.
FIRA was established in 1974 to respond to the concerns of the Canadian people over the ever-increasing foreign control of our economy. In 1973, for instance, foreign investments in Canada totalled $32.9 billion, as against a mere $20.6 billion in the United States, whose economy was then ten times greater.
In 1973 foreign interests, mainly American, were controlling 57 per cent of the Canadian manufacturing industry, 75 per cent of our oil and gas industry and 58 per cent of our mining industry. Surveys had shown that 70 per cent of all Canadians believed our economic opportunities were highly imperilled by such a degree of foreign control.
Over the past ten years, under the previous Liberal administration and thanks to FIRA's efforts, the level of foreign control on Canadian industries and especially the energy sector has decreased significantly. Over the last ten years, although investments have increased from $690 million in 1974 to $2 billion in 1983, the amount of foreign control has declined significantly.
What is the Progressive Conservative Government proposing in its foreign investment policy? First, any new foreign investment will no longer have to be reviewed. Second, any takeover of companies with less than $5 billion in assets may be done automatically. With these two provisions, the Government opens the door to the foreign control of 90 per cent of our industries and companies. Third, in the case of an indirect takeover, or in other words where a foreign company with a Canadian subsidiary is taken over by another foreign company, the transaction will be reviewed only if assets exceed $50 million.
The Progressive Conservative Government is thereby handing over our economy, bound hand and foot, to foreign capital, without concern for the actual impact of foreign investment on this country's economic growth.
Investment Canada Act
Canada is open for business again.

Or rather, as the Bible so aptly puts it, it has sold its birthright for a plate of lentils.

Canada is open for business again.

But the way the Conservatives see it, it is the business of others before ours.
With respect to foreign investments, we ought to know that a great many subsidiary companies of multinationals and quite a few national companies operate under a patent or licence issued by a foreign firm and must do so within the limits of what is called restricted mandates, under which research and development activities, production and international marketing are limited. Restricted mandates quite often specifically ban exports to another country, but the public at large is unaware of this since the companies themselves generally keep such mandates secret. Obviously, those restricted mandates severely hamper Canada's export efforts and we will have to try to have some of those restrictions lifted. Whereas the Liberal government always stressed, through FIRA, the importance of attracting to Canada companies likely to spur our economy, the Conservatives would rather sell out the country to the highest bidder.

Canada is open for business again.

But I ask Mr. Speaker:

For whom? Business for those who tell us that our companies can no longer export as they wish, that they will no longer be able to invest the moneys required for research and development?

Over ten years, FIRA approved more than 90 per cent of investment applications. Rejected applications had often been filed by individuals or companies anxious to do business in Canada and take advantage of our resources without contributing anything to this country's development, since they would have saddled their Canadian subsidiaries with restricted mandates.
Whereas the Conservative government wants to implement a laisser-faire policy which will enable anyone, on any condition, to take over any Canadian company, the Liberal Party of Canada has always emphasized the urgency of securing foreign investments which would create real economic growth in Canada and long-term jobs for Canadians. We believe it is important to have a control mechanism such as FIRA so as to

January 22, 1985
Investment Canada Act
make it possible, among other things, to promote foreign investments in Canada which create subsidiaries with worldwide rather than restricted mandates. It is only because of tariff avantages that subsidiaries locate in a country, and these subsidiaries are fully dependent on the parent company for everything related to product design and product marketing. They will remain in that country only when the tariff advantages are financially beneficial to their investors.
If we want to promote economic growth in our country rather than increase the profits of foreign investors, we do need an agency like FIRA. The point is not to turn down investments offered by multinational companies, but rather to ensure that their subsidiaries have what are commonly called in economics world mandates.
It is the responsibility of the Government to ensure that companies created by foreign investments are independent production bodies which are asked by the parent company to design, manufacture and sell on the world market one or more than one product.
Through its policy, the Liberal Government always tried to encourage companies with world mandates to locate in Canada. You, the Conservatives, have just destroyed ten years of work. Through FIRA, we had always emphasized the international marketing aspect because we know that subsidiaries with a world mandate invest a lot in research and development.

On product design and on product engineering.

With the creation of Investment Canada, small businesses will become choice targets for foreign takeovers. The clause which exempts acquisitions of small businesses from any review is probably the most dangerous clause of this Conservative Bill.
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party will sell public corporations to their most dangerous competitor and allow the acquisition of our small businesses by interests which will take all they can out of them before going somewhere else. [English]
Instead of saying that Canada is open for business, we should say that Canada is ready for a close-out sale by the Conservatives.

Mr. Speaker, I want to participate in this debate on the amendment which effectively hoists Bill C-15 for six months. 1 think that it is a wise amendment because it gives the Government an opportunity to rethink its position.
I do not think there is anyone in this Chamber or this country who did not feel a considerable amount of pride when we repatriated our Constitution. I think that deep down Canadians started to feel a sense of being Canadian, that we can, within the borders of Canada, amend our own Constitution. It was a point of maturity to be able to determine the way
in which our country should be governed. I think that is very important to a sense of being Canadian.
Another aspect of Canadian maturity is the question of controlling our economic destiny; in other words, being in control of our economy and the way it develops and grows. That has been sadly lacking. An example of that is the climbing interest rates in this country in 1982. Pressures were being put on the Government in the House and across the country to do something about rising interest rates. The Government of the day, a Liberal Government, consistently said that it could not do anything about them because they are determined in Washington and on Wall Street. It is the American economy that determines the interest rates in this country. It is the American economy that by and large determines what takes place in this country. We all hoped and prayed that the economic recovery in the United States would be such that their interest rates would come down so that our people could get some relief from high interest rates.
Part of economic maturity is being able to determine where investment coming from outside the borders of Canada should be. We should be able to determine whether those investments ' are in the best interests of Canadians. When I consider my own situation as an immigrant to Canada, I believe it is a privilege to be a Canadian citizen. I realize that there is a contribution which must be made to the life of Canada. We immigrants believe that. I believe we should look at foreign investment in the same way. It should not come in, make a quick buck, rip and run.
I believe there must be a commitment to developing Canada. Of course, investors can derive benefits from this as all Canadians do. Screening foreign investment is important because we cannot assume that our good friend, the United States, can always be trusted. In the past, our good friends have been known to do very unfriendly things to Canadians. For example, the CIA paid money to Canadian psychiatrists to do tests on Canadian citizens.
There are other examples in which foreign parent companies have forbidden the Canadian subsidiary to sell to other countries because the United States Government does not recognize the political philosophy of those other governments. I refer particularly to the sale of Ford vehicles to Cuba. The American Government instructed Ford to instruct its subsidiary here not to sell vehicles because the American Government had an embargo on Cuba. Our former Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, never took such a position yet we had an American law being enforced on a Canadian subsidiary on Canadian soil. We also had the prevention of Robin Hood Flour, a subsidiary in Canada, selling to Red China, as it was called at that time. However, we have recognized the Government of China since 1970.
Those are examples of very unfriendly acts which are sometimes taken by our good friends. Occasionally the Americans get caught up in their own sense of power and view countries like Canada as an extension of themselves. That is a denial of

mature Canadian citizenship and that is why there is a need for screening.
It is interesting to note that the first place the new Progressive Conservative Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) visited after being elected was Washington, to pay a fealty and kiss the ring of king Ronald. The second place he visited outside of our borders was Wall Street, to tell the bankers-
Where it's at.
The Conservative Member on the other side says that's where it's at.
That is right.

He went to assure the bankers that Canada was up for sale. The Conservatives have tried that in Saskatchewan and in British Columbia. British Columbia was opened up by the Social Credit Government of Bill Bennett. It was up for sale. The foreign investors simply came in, ripped and ran. That province today is experiencing one of the most stifling unemployment rates in this country. It is a fantastic province with great potential but is being devastated by unemployment and hard times.
It is quite obvious that the Government is bowing down to the imperialistic monopolies of Wall Street. There is no doubt that they must give some assurance to the money bags of Wall Street that the country is up for sale so that foreign investment will come to Canada. The Government has assured them that foreign investment will not be screened.
Every mature country in the western democracies has some sort of review process. For example, Japan has a very effective review agency. Australia has a foreign review board through which they review foreign investment in their country. Our country needs a proper screening mechanism to ensure that the investments which come to Canada are indeed in the best interest of our country and do not come in to rip, run, rape and take off, leaving Canadians holding the bag.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment to defer the Bill for six months. The recently tabled Investment Canada Act, Bill C-15, represents an attempt by the federal Government to reduce its ability to control and oversee foreign investment in Canada. The consequences of this legislation will reduce the number of transactions subject to review by 90 per cent as compared to the existing FIRA Act. It will totally exempt most new investments from any review and will limit the new agency's mandate to review acquisitions. The net result of this legislation will be an increase in the degree of foreign control over the Canadian economy.
I agree with the member who spoke previously about the-

-the pride of Canadians which is now becoming apparent, and I am all for that.
Investment Canada Act

Since the early 1970s the degree of foreign control has fallen. Part of this change can be attributed to FIRA and to the National Energy Program.
The Government claims that this new Act is intended to reverse the effects of these same programs. Since it is the avowed goal of this new legislation to increase direct foreign investment in Canada, it is useful to consider the implications that foreign domination of our industry might have on the economy. First, let us consider a few aspects of this particular Act. Let us examine the area of culture. There is the right to review all investment in culturally sensitive sectors. While this area has not been clearly defined, it does include the media and telecommunications.

That has me worried because our cultural life is involved, and I should think that at least we must have a broader and more comprehensive definition if we are to preserve what makes us different as Canadians.

Second, research and development. It has been argued that Canada suffers from a technologically weak manufacturing sector, that this sector is small in size relative to the Canadian economy, by OECD standards, and undertakes less research and development than other industrialized nations. According to data presented in the New Directions for Canada, Canadian private R and D funding ranks last at .8 per cent among the OECD countries. The Science Council of Canada has long noted that there is a strong relationship between our poor R and D performance and the level of foreign ownership in the economy. International companies tend to concentrate their R and D activity and the location of this activity in either the home country or where the largest market is located. Both of these factors work against Canadian R and D activity and I believe that this is a very serious concern.
According to the Science Council of Canada, foreign-owned firms engage in significantly less research here than do Canadian-owned firms. As foreign ownership increases and displaces Canadian firms, employment opportunities for our labour force in this area will fall. What will happen to all of our students who are presently studying in the field of science and research? This must be considered. Will we be concerned about a brain drain and perhaps not think about what the impact of this will be on research and development?
In this respect it is particularly relevant to note that the acquisition of small enterprises is exempt from review under this new Investment Canada Act. Yet it is precisely these firms which tend to be the most R and D intensive and innovative in the economy. This may be a particular danger in the high-tech area where we have shown tremendous expertise. Consider our pride in the Canadarm when our space shots took off. It is small innovative firms such as those, many of which are below the $5 million threshold set by the Minister, which will suffer the impact of the legislation. Something concrete will be lost. What will be gained? That is a very important key.

January 22, 1985
Investment Canada Act
I think we need this delay so we can really research the impact that this Act will have on Canada as an independent country. Having other U.S. firms buy up small Canadian corporations, meld them into their own over-all organization and withdraw them from the Canadian labour force I think is detrimental to ourselves. This Bill does nothing for small business, which we all know is the major key to regrowth and development in Canada. It is that very proof that we count on to revitalize our economy.
I want to emphasize that the Liberal Party is not against foreign investment. We welcome foreign investors, but as partners in the Canadian economy, not as controllers of our financial destiny. Through FIRA, which may have had a bad reputation but did not have bad results, the previous Government was able to negotiate benefits for Canadian workers. This Bill does away with a safeguard that I believe is necessary if Canada is not going to become the handmaiden of the United States. Our Leader has said time and again that we are open for business but we are not for sale. I want to re-emphasize that. I think we must maintain our Canadian perspective.
According to Glen Williams of Carleton University, Canadian branch plants have experienced a long history of export restrictions by their American parents with probably 75 per cent of all Canadian branch plants having their exports strictly controlled by their parent. This can be a serious matter for a country like Canada which relies so heavily on exports for our national income.
Look at the Americans who have complained loudest and have been the most protectionist of their interests. A recent study by the Brookings Institute demonstrates that the percentage of U.S. manufactured goods protected by non-tariff restrictions, such as quotas and other barriers, has risen from 20 per cent in 1980 to 35 per cent in 1983. The truth is the United States is as economically nationalist as we are here in Canada.
What the Tories have attempted to do with this Bill is to repackage a piece of legislation that in reality worked quite well. In the past five years, over 92 per cent of all applications for FIRA were approved. This is a perception that the legislation was an impediment to foreign investment, but these statistics do not bear that out.
Let us take a look at what a well-known journalist from the Toronto Star has said. He wrote that the Minister of Regional Development had announced that 90 per cent of all foreign investment transactions will no longer be reviewed. The criterion of "significant" benefit will be replaced by "net" benefit. Investment Canada will now actively seek out foreign investors rather than bargaining with them for the best deal; and instead of the full Cabinet deciding on the 10 per cent of large takeovers that even the Tories deemed to be too important to leave to the market, those decisions will now be made by the Minister alone. One single Minister will rule on billion dollar decisions. The biases of one man will decide the fate of thousands of workers or the interests of entire regions. There has not been such an imbalance between power and capability
since Caligula made a counsel out of his horse. I think that is a very important aspect of this Bill. I do not think that is what Members of this House expected, and I do not think that is what Canadian electors voted for when they voted for change. That is not a very democratic process.
I would like to bring to the attention of Hon. Members that other factors also have an impact. Regulations, both federal and provincial, have a direct bearing on the level of foreign investment in Canada. It is not enough just to change FIRA which represents only one layer of the various strata that govern our economy. The constraints are not addressed by this Bill nor have they been alluded to or addressed by the Minister. Maybe they have escaped his focus and myopic view of Canadian problems. We need increased productivity, true, and access to foreign markets, yes-jobs, growth and development. But when one has a fixation on setting climate with words and chooses to ignore the many factors that impact on our economic weather patterns, the forecast is clouded and unreliable.
I see my time is running out. I would really like to press you, Mr. Speaker, to consider the other factors that have been very important in having businessmen make decisions. I would like to underscore the importance of Canadians being encouraged to invest in Canada. We have experienced the flight of capital.

speechtext: Now that was the Liberal Government.

I think there are ways in which we can prevent that and encourage Canadians to invest in Canada as well. I think the fixation is misplaced. All kinds of other issues are integral to the creating of a favourable climate, such as taxation structure, labour atmosphere, regulations and the availability of trained manpower. Regarding taxation, it is heaviest in Canada and certainly in Quebec.
In conclusion, I want to reiterate that we on this side of the House welcome foreign capital into Canada if it is going to improve our economy, help create jobs and be of significant benefit to Canada. Unfortunately, there is very little evidence in this Bill to substantiate these claims. I think we really need to have this delay so we can examine this legislation much more closely, legislation which appears to be like any other Tory charade and like the many the Tories played out in the election campaign on universality and jobs, jobs, jobs. The Minister's rhetoric is just a smokescreen which will soon disappear, leaving behind the real problems that still need to be addressed by this Government.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this Bill that will have the effect of limiting Canadian control over investment in this nation. I rise to speak with three different roles in mind: first, as federal-provincial relations critic for our caucus; second, as the labour spokesman for our caucus; and third, as a constituency Member of Parliament. In all three roles I am concerned about this piece of legislation.
As the federal-provincial relations critic I am concerned that with this legislation neither the provinces nor the federal Government will be able to control or regulate the economies
January 22, 1985

of their various jurisdictions. We will be in a situation, as has so often been the case in Canada, where the real decisions that affect the development of our economy, that affect the employment prospects of our children and the development of our resources, will be made elsewhere. In other words, they will be made in other nations, in the board rooms of companies that are basically offshore.
It has been evident from past foreign investment in this country that Canadians have suffered as a result of foreign investment. Sure, there have been some jobs created. Sure, there has been some research and development. Sure, there has been some extraction of our natural resources and as a result there has been some benefit to Canada. But there are other statistics as well. Those statistics will point out that where there is foreign ownership there will not be as much research and development. They will point out that where there is foreign ownership there are more layoffs than there should be in comparison to what has happened in Canadian-owned firms. There are statistics that will show we have been a net loser in terms of interest and dividend payments ever since 1926. For that matter, in 1983 we had a loss of $9.4 billion which had to be paid to companies other than Canadian nationals. What that meant was a dollar drain on our economy, dollars that should have been used for more research and development, for more investment and for more jobs for Canadians.
We have also seen historically that foreign-owned corporations tend to do less manufacturing with our natural resources. In other words, they tend to take the natural product from the ground and move it in an unrefined state to their headquarters or to factories in other nations. If we had Canadian control over those corporations there would be more opportunity for secondary and tertiary employment of Canadians.
We are allowed to speak for only 10 minutes in this debate. That is unfortunate because there are a number of points I would like to make. However, I will talk about something now which affects all of us, whether we be on this side of the House or on the opposite side of the House. Last October I wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about a study of the Science Council of Canada. Certainly it was not done by a group of socialists or labour people; it was done by the Science Council of Canada and it examined the role of foreign investment over the last many years that the Liberals were in power. It contains some very interesting conclusions. First, it indicated that by and large foreign firms did not match the research and development dollars which they received from the federal Government or from provincial Governments. At the same time Canadian-owned firms were matching on a dollar for dollar basis the money they received from Governments.
That study was conducted by Frank Longo for the Science Council of Canada. It established that this was the pattern over the last many years in this nation. In other words, foreign firms would take the tax benefits, grants or whatever they could get from government and use them for some research and development but would not put in their own money. Any
Investment Canada Act
research and development conducted with their own money would be done in nations other than Canada.
What does that mean to Canadians? It means that research and development was not done here. It means that Canadians are less likely to receive the benefits of research and development. Also it means that young people lose the possibility of working in research and development because most of the money spent by foreign-owned firms in being spent elsewhere. Canadians either lose the opportunity or they must leave Canada to work in research and development in those corporations. Also it means that the many jobs resulting from R and D will not be located in Canada. We are the losers in many ways when corporations refuse to do research and development in Canada.
There is another interesting aspect of the Longo study. It was that the vast majority of foreign-owned firms did significantly less research and development with or without government grants than Canadian companies. In other words, they do not match the money they receive from the Government of Canada or from the provincial Goverments, although Canadian-owned firms at least match that money for research and development purposes, and in addition, these foreign firms, by and large, do not do as much research and development in the nation. This study for the Science Council of Canada which is headed by the former leader of the provincial Liberal Party in Ontario. He is not known for left-wing, radical thought. For that matter, on many issues he has been proven to be to the right of the Conservative Party.
Now, now!

I know that is hard to believe, but certainly there are some Liberals who are right of the Conservative Party. The point is that that study examined the record of the previous federal Liberal administration. It pointed out that we were losing research and development dollars because of foreign investment and that the youth of the nation were losing opportunities because of foreign investment.
What is the Conservative Government doing about that? It says that even though the weak controls of the past were not working, they have to be disbanded and further weakened so that we have less control in the future.
I come from a riding with many natural resources. There is high unemployment among women, the youth and native people. The fact that there will be less control over foreign-owned corporations, which control so much of the industries and companies in the field of natural resources, means that we will have even less control or less say in the future in terms of what happens in Canada, particularly what happens in my riding.
For this reason I believe the amendment to postpone discussion on this Bill for six months is a good one. Then we could examine not only the studies of the Science Council of Canada but other information which proves that we cannot afford to weaken the very limited controls we have at the present time.

Investment Canada Act

Mr. Speaker, I, too, am pleased to take part in the debate on our Party's amendment to Bill C-15. Parliament and the country needs that time to review this piece of legislation. Essentially the Bill will dismantle FIRA, to make way for a proposed new investment instrument which will be known as Investment Canada and thereby dramatically alter the process by which acquisitions are to be addressed by the new Tory Government.
In reality Bill C-15 is yet another attempt by a government far more interested in the art of public relations than in actual substance, a government prepared to sacrifice long-term economic planning and economic sovereignty for short-term, image-making propaganda.
The Minister who introduced the legislation late last year declared the following in his press statement:
We are back in business. This legislation sends a message to the world that, once again, Canada welcomes investment.
Of what world did the Minister speak? Where has he been for the last number of years? This country has always been open for business and has always welcomed investment. If this were not the case, we would not be witness to what is, on the whole, a very great, prosperous and thriving nation. In terms of economic investment, under a Liberal Government and through FIRA specifically Canada like any other country wanted and stressed what was good for Canada and for Canadians. Is that a negative attitude to take as a country? Is not that how a country attains a degree of respect in the international business community?
FIRA, introduced by a Liberal Government, was an essential and calculated policy instrument which sought to ensure that foreign investment also included significant benefits to Canada. FIRA allowed Canadians to bargain and negotiate with a huge variety of multinational interests from a point of strength. A case in point was the 86 per cent share of Canadian Reserve Oil and Gas Ltd. which Getty Oil acquired in 1980. Getty's initial application to FIRA in 1981 was rejected. Serious negotiation followed, which resulted in a stronger package for Canada being approved only a year later. This package included commitments by Getty to reduce its ownership of the Canadian company to 50 per cent and to spend $5 million in four years developing known reserves. It also agreed to spend many millions of dollars over a period of years on exploration and development. The company also agreed to buy Canadian goods and services whenever they were competitively available and to sponsor scholarships in Canadian universities. Finally, residents of Canadian origin had to make up 80 per cent of the directors of both companies. Getty was required to transfer technology to Canadian reserves and to spend money on research in Canada.
In this illustration, it is very clear that FIRA had an important role in ensuring that this foreign investment was totally beneficial to Canada in addition to satisfying the investor.
The objective of FIRA was never to prevent or discourage foreign investment, but rather to cater to the needs and aspirations of our country. It should be noted that since its inception in 1974, as was previously mentioned, FIRA approved an average of 92 per cent of the applications. This figure clearly demonstrates that foreign investors not only wanted to invest and did invest heavily in Canada, but that they were willing to meet the criteria established by FIRA. In short, these investors realized and appreciated that more jobs for Canadians, more research and development for Canada and greater Canadian exports was part of the investment deal. Our Party and Canadians are asking themselves, why should it be any different today?
It is doubtful whether FIRA discouraged in any significant way any foreign investor who was serious about investing his or her capital in Canada. In fact, the Conference Board of Canada, in a study last April, determined that FIRA provided a deterrent for only 11 per cent of foreign investment. This was tied largely to the time factor.
More importantly, Statistics Canada figures indicate that FIRA did not halt the flow of U.S. investment into Canada. In fact, the gross inflow of U.S. direct investment into Canada continued to expand during FIRA's time. Gross inflows varied between $1 billion and $1.4 billion throughout most of the 1970s before skyrocketing during 1980 and 1981.
Therefore, a quick analysis of the facts and figures effectively contradicts the Government's blinded portrayal that FIRA was the enemy of foreign investment and that the removal of FIRA, replaced by Investment Canada, would bring a new beginning. Nothing could be further from the truth.
As the Bill stands, direct acquisitions by non-Canadians of businesses in Canada with assets of less than $5 million are not subject to review. Neither are indirect takeovers resulting from the acquisition of parent companies outside Canada when the Canadian subsidiary has assets of over $50 million. This is of grave concern to the Canadian small-businessman, particularly in the increasingly competitive field of high technology. The Government will open the doors to takeovers of firms below these thresholds. What will Canada really gain if these small enterprises are more prone to shut-downs? What would we gain if these Canadian jobs are not guaranteed? What steps will be available to the Canadian Government to prevent such economic hardships? What action can the Government take to guarantee benefits to Canada and to ensure jobs for all Canadians? Unfortunately, the answer to these and other questions is that this Government wishes to wash its hands of its commitment to the small-businessman.
These economic concessions will no longer be possible through Investment Canada. Many firms that are below the new thresholds may in fact be small, but collectively they are the engine and the spirit behind the creation of new jobs in Canada.
To further compound the inequities of Investment Canada, the larger takeovers which dictate the fate of thousands of
January 22, 1985

Canadian workers and the interests of entire regions will now rest at the mercy of one single Minister. Under FIRA, these would be shared by the full Cabinet in order to incorporate and understand the variety of disciplines, interests and regional necessities. The perspective, in the end, was much more encompassing. Now, a billion dollar decision in the hands of one single Minister centralizes power to an unprecedented degree and with it imposes horrendous limitation as it relates to the spectrum of interests.
Not only is the concept that FIRA discouraged foreign investment a fabricated myth perpetuated by the Tories, but this inaccuracy is also complemented by a feeling that at the present time the United States is least likely to undergo active investment abroad. This growing view was echoed in a fascinating article in The Globe and Mail dated December 20, 1984, in which leading New York investment bankers claim that "those waiting for job-producing foreign moneys to flow into Canada should not hold their breath. You don't get the idea that there are a lot of folks with money bags at the border, waiting to get into Canada".
Consequently, when you combine this limited investment attitude with the reality that FIRA did not discourage foreign investment, one asks why Bill C-15, and how can we grow and profit as a nation from the establishment of Investment Canada? Investment Canada is the first major piece of Government legislation and it provides Canadians very quickly with the philosophical bent that handcuffs the Conservative Party. A debate of FIRA versus Investment Canada is a classic example which distinguishes a Liberal Government from that of a Conservative Government.
Firstly, FIRA was an instrument of nation building; an instrument to safeguard and promote Canadians and Canadian economic sovereignty. Investment Canada will do neither. Secondly, while foreign investment was viewed as an indispensable sector of the economic pie, FIRA was an initiative by Canadians to put Canadians first; it was an initiative that attempted to instil a sense of purpose, vitality and leadership. Investment Canada will merely perpetuate the often heard criticism that Canada lacks the drive and self-fortitude to make things happen. Thirdly, FIRA put Canada second to no one; it viewed Canada and the United States as co-tenants of the North American continent. Investment Canada views the U.S. as the owner and Canada as the subservient tenant.
I have other things to say, but I believe my time is up.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to rise on behalf of my constituents of Nepean-Carleton to speak against this amendment and in support of the Bill. This Bill recognizes that investment is central to economic growth and employment opportunities and the key to technological advancement.
I could hardly believe some of the speeches which preceded me this morning in support of FIRA, particularly when the Canadian Press last week carried an article with which I would like Hon. Members to be familiar entitled: "Canada ranked worst". I quote:
Investment Canada Act
A survey released Monday on the international competitiveness of 28 countries ranks Canada as the seventh-most competitive country, but dead last in terms of welcoming foreign investment.
The survey repeated oft-heard criticisms that Canadians are probably the world's most unfriendly recipients of foreign investments.
Presumably FIRA has contributed dramatically to this kind of perception by those who want to invest in Canada. In the case of Nepean-Carleton, a riding that is comprised in large part of small businesses, a riding that is the high technology centre for Canada, this new investment Bill is particularly welcome. The high technology industry must raise capital quickly. Twelve to 18 months is crucial for the turnaround period in that industry. Equally important is the desirability of cross-licensing within the high technology industry and of being able to move with cross-licensing very quickly. The small business industry and the high technology industry in Nepean-Carleton very much want this new Bill to be operative as soon as possible.
I would like to direct my comments for a few minutes to how the new Bill affects the mining industry in Canada. I am particularly delighted that the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton) is in the Chamber today. This Government and this nation are particularly fortunate in having this Member to provide the legislative and policy leadership for Canada's great mining community.
We are the third largest mining community in the world, ranking after the United States and the Soviet Union. At the minehead or at the millhead, we produce approximately $33 billion to $35 billion of new wealth annually. That new wealth constitutes about 30 per cent of Canada's net exports. It is a very, very competitive industry. It is an industry that is being confronted with an array of problems, many of which relate to the investment community. I would like to share some of these problems with you for a moment.
In Canada, it is now taking about four to five years to find every new ranking ore deposit. That exploration program, when related back to each new find, is costing about $25 million to $30 million per deposit. Equally, in these worldranking mining institutions the cost of developing these mines is anywhere from $200 million to $400 million, a colossal amount of capital for anyone's investment portfolio.
In the mining industry there is a need for an inflow of large amounts of capital. Superimposed upon that need is also something which this House and those of us who are responsible for legislation relative to the mining industry ought to note, and that is that there is a tremendous time factor associated with the development of a mine. Exploration takes three to five years. The planning of a new operation takes another two to three years and it takes probably at least another five years to bring a major mining complex into production by developing the mine, the mill, the community infrastructure and everything else that is associated with it. The mine then enters into production and it needs a period of at least 10, 15 or 20 years of stability so that that mine can produce.
