Investment Canada Act
The point I would like to make is that from the time one starts to invest one's money in the mining community to the time one receives the total return on that mine, a period of at least 20 to 30 years can go by. Therefore, there is a need for stability in the tax system and in the investment world for the mining community to grow and thrive.
One of the great problems from which the mining community has suffered over the years, beginning in about 1971, 1972 and 1973 is the bewildering array of legislation which applies to taxation and investment. That has tended to hinder this great industry, slow it down and give it a lack of confidence in what Canadian legislators and policymakers would want from the industry. I hope that through this new Bill that is before us we as legislators can provide the Canadian mining community with an opportunity to attract large amounts of new capital into Canada and that we will very shortly defeat the amendment that is before us and proceed with this very valuable piece of legislation which the business, high-technology and mining communities in Canada, and in fact all Canadians, need so desperately.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I too welcome the opportunity to participate in debate regarding the amendment introduced by the Liberal Party to put a six-month hoist on Bill C-15, the Bill dealing with foreign investment in Canada. After hearing the addresses of some of the Hon. Members of this House, I am somewhat amazed- though I suppose I should not be - by the fact that some of the economic theories that I have heard are really 19th century economic theories, as is the understanding of political and economic realities. I also find amazing some of the speeches I have heard by my Liberal colleagues. On the one hand they take great credit for FIRA, yet on the other hand they bend over backward to point out how FIRA has not in fact stopped or interfered with foreign investment in Canada.
I believe all those who recognize the political history of the country know that it was the New Democratic Party which, in the early 1970s, really created the public and political pressure within this House that forced the Liberals to introduce FIRA to begin with. Since then we have seen an erosion of FIRA over the last number of years.
It is not surprising at all that in the last number of years FIRA has been approving some 95 per cent to 98 per cent of all foreign-investor takeovers in Canada. It is not surprising that after all these years of Liberal rule and management-or I should say mismanagement-of our economy we find that, per capita, Canada has more foreign ownership and control than any other industrialized nation in the world and more than many developing nations as well. That is why I was somewhat surprised when I heard the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper) claiming that Canada is considered the country that is the most unreceptive to foreign investment. Oh boy, that is some unreceptivity!
This country or at least a great deal of it is already controlled by foreign investment. We have more foreign ownership than any other industrialized nation in the world on a per capita basis. Yet this is not quite good enough for our Conservative friends. How much do they want? Do they want 100 per cent foreign ownership? Do they just want to sell it all? Do they want us to be totally controlled by multinational corporations? Do they want Canada's economy to be a totally subservient branch plant economy? How much more do they want? How much further must we go? How much more should we sell out? Do we not already hold the world record for this?
I wish some of my Conservative colleagues would tell us how much more foreign investment they would like to see. There is no doubt that foreign investment is needed. However, I am speaking of the type of foreign investment that is needed. Let me put it this way. As an individual, I could rent for most of my life and end up never owning my own home. On the other hand, I could borrow money from the bank, put a down payment on a home and eventually pay it off. Then I would own my home, the roof over my head. But what has occurred in our country is that we have become renters or tenants in our own homes. We will never end up owning the factories, the mines or the mills. We continue paying rent. That is why in 1983 Canada had a deficit of some $9.4 billion in interest and dividend payments.
Since the record began in 1926, Canada has been a net exporter of interest and dividend funds. In other words, while foreign investment provides short-term immediate benefits, people do not invest unless they expect to receive more out of it than they put in. That is simple Adam Smith economics. I am sure my Conservative friends can appreciate that anyone who invests in Canada expects to get more out of it. That has been the case. More dividends and interest payments from past investments are leaving Canada than are coming back in. If the solution is to borrow more money to make up the difference, we are only mortgaging the future.
I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker. I wish to continue with my remarks later this afternoon.

The Minister of Veterans Affairs did not know anything about the speech which was delivered by the Minister of National Defence at NATO, but he assured the House that the Minister did make a very good statement at NATO, and also assured the House that what he had said made a great deal of sense, even though he did not know what the Minister had said.
As the record has since shown, the Minister of National Defence was in fact making use of decisions which were made by the previous Liberal Government, and the new equipment which was purchased by the previous Liberal Government, to try to give the impression to NATO that this brand new Government was doing such a fantastic job. In his statement before NATO, the Minister of National Defence is quoted as having said:
We are completing project definition for the acquisition of weapons to enable our forces in Europe to counter the threat of tow level air attack. We are replacing our CF-104 aircraft in Europe with far more capable CF-18 aircraft on a one-for-one basis. We intend, with the transition to the new aircraft, to increase both the operational readiness and the operational capability of the Canadian Air Group-
I would advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, livestock producers in the Maritime region are recommending that feed freight assistance be increased by the federal Government to a level which will ensure that producers are in a fair and competitive position with the remainder of Canada.
In 1941 the Feed Freight Assistance Program covered 90 per cent of freight costs incurred in bringing feed grain into the Maritimes. However, by 1984 assistance only covered 20 per cent of the cost of importing feed. During the same time period freight costs increased fourfold, and this has resulted in unfair feed grain prices in eastern Canada. The cost of producing a hog is now $20 higher in the Maritimes than in Ontario, because of the feed cost difference.
Obviously the survival of the maritime hog industry is threatened, and a heavy burden is also placed upon dairy, poultry, beef, and sheep producers.
Left unattended, we stand to lose 4,000 to 5,000 jobs in our livestock and food processing industries over the next few years. I therefore ask the Government to implement a feed cost equalization plan for imported western and Ontario grain, and for imported protein concentrates. In addition, I would recommend that Agriculture Canada establish a schedule of bonus payments to Maritime producers for high production levels in feed grain and protein crops.

Mr. Speaker, an unfortunate tradition which was practised continually by previous Liberal Governments is being continued by the Conservative Government. That tradition, the appointment by the Prime Minister of old friends and supporters to positions of influence and power, was sustained during the Christmas recess when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made over 90 appointments, including 24 top level bureaucracy jobs and 66 to other bodies such as boards, commissions, and that dusty old place, the Senate.
Decidedly obvious by their absence were the ethnic appointments the Prime Minister promised he would make. He was quoted as saying:
The Progressive Conservative Party of Canada will appoint competent and qualified men and women who reflect our cultural diversity to positions on government boards, agencies. Crown corporations and the senior Public Service.
Now, more and more Canadians are asking themselves and the Prime Minister: "When?" Indeed, the only appointment of a Canadian from our ethnic communities of over eight million people was that of the Saskatchewan neurologist, Dr. Efstathios Barootes, to the Senate.
The Prime Minister is reportedly furious that he has not been given the names of more members of visible communities in Canada from which to choose. Yet we are told by the President of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council, Mr. Navin Parekh, that he himself submitted 70 resumes of his most qualified members to the Prime Minister's appointment chief. Not one of those candidates has received an appointment to date.
Is the Prime Minister, in his failure to appoint any of these people, saying that they are not qualified to serve Canada? I honestly hope not.

I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, on October 17, 1984, at approximately 3.30 p.m., a Piper Cheyenne aircraft, No. C-GAPT, crashed on the approach to the Lester B. Pearson International Airport, killing all on board. While any loss of life in a situation such as this is a tragedy, the successful past and the brilliant future of the owner, Grenville Martin, makes it doubly distressing. When, as it now appears from all reports, the pilot had been cheating on his medical examinations, the waste of life is even more senseless.
I ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) to consider seriously sending a reference to the Standing Committee on Transport asking it, either in whole or through a sub-committee, to investigate and report on the seriousness of this kind of cheating, and to recommend ways in which it might be eliminated.

not do their research here. They do it back home in the country of the parent firm, which is usually the United States.
In a report that was released earlier this fall by the Science Council of Canada entitled The Canadian Industrial Development: Some Policy Directions, the effects of the multinationals on research and development in Canada are discussed. What do we find? We find that the branch plants operating in Canada have lower productivity than Canadian firms. Let me read the following from that report:
A comparison of the productivity of industries in Canada with that of their counterparts in the United States showed that, for manufacturing, the productivity gap between the two countries is about 25 per cent. A number of factors contribute to poor productivity performance in Canada, but possibly the most surprising is the effect of foreign control. As Saunders has found, high foreign control of an industry in Canada contributes to Canada's poor productivity performance.
I find it surprising that the Government looks at more foreign control as the economic solution to the mess in which Canada finds itself. Surely that is not the road to follow when solving our long-term problems. The solution surely lies in becoming more self-sufficient within this country. It lies in being able to produce the goods and services that we need for ourselves. It means taking a different approach toward becoming self-sufficient. It means taking an approach toward developing new types of technologies, new types of research and development in areas that would allow for small-scale production that is as efficient, if not more efficient, than large-scale production. It means following a road on which we begin to conserve the capital that is available in this country. It means moving down the road toward decentralization, community control and control by workers. It means a new vision for Canada. It does not mean a continuation of the Liberal vision which sees us becoming a branch plant economy under the large economic unit of the United States. It means that we truly become masters in our own house.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are indicating to me that my time is up. I have a few minutes left and would seek the unanimous consent of the House to allow me to continue with my remarks and be able to conclude them.
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to take part in this important debate in the House on foreign investment in Canada. I firmly believe that Canada should not become a mere warehouse for foreign corporations. We all realize that foreign investment is important to Canada's growth, but the Government must remain vigilant and ensure that new foreign investment will have a long-term beneficial impact on the entire country. Unfortu-
Investment Canada Act
nately, eliminating FIRA and replacing it by a blank cheque, as it were, means that large American corporations will ignore the wishes of Canadians and thumb their noses at policies designed to protect and promote Canadian interests.
I shall, if I may, give a short history of foreign investment in Canada to illustrate the shortcomings of Bill C-15. In the past, a number of reports have been tabled in the House, describing the harmful effects of letting foreign investment infiltrate Canada's economy. We had the Gorden Report in 1957, the Watkins Report in 1968, the Hahn Report in 1970 and finally the Gray Report in 1972. Mr. Speaker, all these studies described major problems arising from extensive control of our economy by foreign corporations.
In fact, before 1974, the drawbacks of extensive foreign control included the proliferation of branch plants, the effect being to reduce competition by setting up oligopolies within Canadian industry.
American anti-trust legislation prevented corporations from modernizing and upgrading their branches, thus leading to low productivity, greater inefficiency and higher prices for the consumer.
There was also the matter of branch profits that were siphoned away to the parent corporations outside Canada instead of being reinvested in this country. This was done in various ways, such as establishing transfer prices or through abnormal imports.
There is also the manner in which the branch is controlled by the parent corporation. Branches are often excluded from international production contracts and are run in accordance with decisions taken in a foreign country.
Furthermore, many branches have no research and development facilities, their only purpose being to assemble and sell their products. I may refer to the excellent point made on another occasion in the House by the Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), who stated that the total amount of research and development done by Canadian corporations is five times that done by foreign corporations located in Canada. The House is of course aware that research and development are a vital part of Canada's economy growth and economic renewal.
Those were the main problems arising from the excessive powers wielded by foreign-controlled corporations within the Canadian economy before the creation of FIRA.
In 1974, the Foreign Investment Review Agency was created by the Government to deal with the problems I have just mentioned.
Foreign investment proposals were examined by Cabinet to ensure they presented a significant benefit for Canada. The review process was supposed to consider five criteria. First, the effect of the investment on the level and nature of economic activity in Canada, including employment, resource processing

January 22, 1985
Investment Canada Act
and exports. Second, the degree and significance of participation by Canadians in the business enterprise and in the industry to which the enterprise belongs. Third, the effect on productivity, industrial efficiency, technological development, product innovation and product variety, another set of criteria that were used to determine whether an investment was justified. Fourth, the effect on competition, and fifth and last, the compatibility of the investment with national industrial and economic policies, taking into consideration industrial and economic policy objectives enunciated by the provinces likely to be significantly affected by the investment.
Mr. Speaker, when FIRA was created, the Americans did not take offence. The United States ambassador at the time, Mr. Thomas Enders, said the following in May 1979: "We were afraid that FIRA would be an obstacle to new investment in Canada. However, we have found that FIRA has been faithful to its mandate, which was to ensure that investment proposals contain certain benefits for Canada". The U.S. ambassador went on to say: "The Agency's present approval rate of 90 per cent is an indication of the quality of the proposals it receives". The ambassador also said: "I understand Canada's position, as a country that is so heavily dependent on foreign investment, that it finds it necessary to have such a mechanism to ensure that its interests are known and respected."
Mr. Speaker, this was said by a representative of the United States who, in 1979, was not making a big thing about the existence of FIRA. However, FIRA has clearly been effective, and Canadians have benefited from this legislation.
Yes it is true that afterwards, on the other side of the border, criticism was levelled at FIRA, but the negative remarks had to do with FIRA's procedural requirements and administrative difficulties rather than on the right or even the obligation of Canada to ensure that foreign investments were more properly geared to our interests.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, the new government seems more interested in kowtowing to the United States than in solving problems related to a foreign-controlled economy.
According to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), the new agency, Investment Canada, will be given:
-a new positive mandate to promote and encourage investments.
After reading the Bill, I can see that the Minister is interested in two things: the United States and more wide-ranging powers for himself.
According to Bill C-15, the new investment proposals to be reviewed will have to bear the approval of the Minister rather than the Cabinet, as was the case with FIRA. In other words, the opinion of one person will decide about takeovers which will create or eliminate thousands of jobs for Canadians. The objectivity-the political will, in fact-will be the exclusive realm of one Minister who will make decisions within the
confidential confines of his office. That is far too much responsibility and power for one Minister, particularly when one knows who will be the Minister responsible for FIRA or Investment Canada. Mr. Speaker, giving that responsibility to the Minister is somewhat like putting Dracula in charge of a blood bank.
And how!

The Minister has replaced the concept of significant benefit by the concept of net benefit. In other words, the government is more concerned about making profitable investments than ensuring that Canada's foreign trade is in our own interest. It used to be that we were in a position to negotiate and make foreign investments as profitable as possible for Canada. But now the Americans can come to Canada and do practically anything they like. While the Minister responsible extends a welcoming hand to the United States, the Americans are threatening to raise non-tariff barriers against Canadian products.
I see Members opposite and I am sure that they have hog producers among their constituents. They ought to realize that kowtowing to the Americans is not going to do wonders for hog exporters. I am quite concerned about the way things are going and about those Ministers who are walking on their knees before President Reagan and American interest groups that want to continue to control Canada. On the other hand, we find out that all kinds of barriers are raised against Canadian products going to American markets. We now find out that they have been walking on their knees without asking for anything in return. Mr. Speaker, that is not what I call negotiations.
We have heard the Secretary of State for External Affairs give full support to President Reagan and his star war. Well, Mr. Speaker, you know very well that the Secretary of State for external Affairs does not have enough imagination to think in terms of a strictly Canadian policy.
Once again he thinks that following in the footsteps of the United States is the correct approach for Canada. Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that, with Investment Canada and the kowtowing of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, they are destroying the independence, sovereignty and pride of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I had an opportunity to listen to some of my colleagues on both sides of the House who were addressing the amendment to Bill C-15. I have to say that I unalterably oppose it.
I was surprised at the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) who spoke about Canada giving everything to the United States, Canada's largest trading partner. Obviously he was talking about a country which he does not seem to realize is the most powerful nation in the world. He does not seem to realize that we are its neighbour and principal trading partner.
January 22, 1985

The Hon. Member does not seem to realize that Canada has bonds which do not weld it inextricably together with the United States, but that there are bonds which weld us together in many other contexts-in a cultural sense, in a linguistic sense and in multicultural composition.
I had an opportunity to examine and to consider the comments which were made by the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). Before he called it one o'clock he made some rather strange allegations about foreign investment. He stated-perhaps accurately so; I have not seen the figures-that of all the industrialized nations Canada has the greatest component of foreign investment. Obviously, in his mind that is bad. He went on to say that Canada has a greater component of foreign investment than some Third World countries. So what? I can think of some Third World countries in which no one in their right mind would care to invest because those countries are so politically volatile and unstable.
We listen to the NDP, with its clarion call and its shrill voice about nationalism, bemoaning foreign investment on the one hand, and then on the other endorsing Weyerhaeuser in acquiring the timber limits which it has in British Columbia. It endorses Weyerhaeuser in the United States and denies Canadian participation. There was a Canadian group which was prepared to take over the operation at the time Weyerhaeuser applied. Whom did the NDP support? It supported the U.S. application. It is a matter of record and I would challenge any Member on the other side to prove otherwise. What was wrong with that? I would say that there was nothing wrong. Weyerhaeuser happened to be one of the very few good managers of the forest sector.
I could provide a better example, that of St. Regis Pulp and Paper. It is an American company which is based in New York and operates in Hinton. It has one of the largest forest nurseries that can be found. At any time that company will not have to go any farther than 45 miles in order to cut trees. It is in a northern climate, it has an excellent nursery system and an ongoing system of silviculture which could well be emulated by the forest industries in Canada which are Canadian-owned and operated.
Those Members from British Columbia who know anything about the forest sector should know whereof I speak. But St. Regis Pulp and Paper is an American company and for some reason it has to have some shadow over it. There has to be some cloud or some element of doubt and concern in the heads of the NDP Members because of that. Well, their economic nationalism is fine until they get to the point of explaining to Canadians that they are going to have to undergo a very serious reduction in their lifestyle and standard of living if we deny the foreign investment they would have us deny.
I listened to the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) earlier today talking about Conservatives going out of their way to draw in foreign investment. He did not give us the other side. He did not tell us about his own Government going out of its way to drive foreign investment out of Canada, aided
Investment Canada Act
and abetted by the NDP. They created the National Energy Program and not only killed the largest single tax-paying component of the industrial sector of Canada, they also killed off thousands of jobs for blue-collar Canadian workers in the Alberta oil patch. They did that very successfully.
The NDP Members say that they are well informed on that subject. They are so well informed, Mr. Speaker, that the former energy critic for the NDP did not know the difference between heavy oil and tar sands when he talked to people from Alberta. That is how well informed they are. Let us face the fact that obviously the Opposition is unaware of the FIRA process. It is unaware that an application involving $4,000 to take over a car wash in Windsor had to have Cabinet approval. What stupidity. What a waste of the time and talent of any Cabinet. Just a total and absolute waste. Then there was the fellow from Massachusetts who wanted to provide a certain component in the programming sector of the computer industry. One small businessman with a small investment. How long did he wait for a decision, because that intrusion into Canada might have had a horrendous effect on our economy? That gentleman waited ten months for a Cabinet decision. That is the kind of thing that fits the mind-set of the opposition Members. That is the kind of thing they can understand. They know what the bureaucracy is. They live with it, they love it, they created it. But that is not the way we want to operate. That is not the way we intend to operate. We intend to give Canadians the opportunity for jobs which can only be created by, in part, encouraging that foreign investment component.
I would now ask the NDP and the Liberals to give me their answer about the auto makers. Where do Canadian auto workers stand on this position? Tell me about General Motors, Ford, Chrysler and others. Tell me about those and other American giants operating in Canada. I mean, I am sure I could have caught one of those dear fellows sitting down eating a Big Mac from McDonald's. That is a bad name because it is an American name. Well, they take you right from the sublime to the ridiculous. They talk about state of the art. I can tell you what their policies are, Mr. Speaker, they are state of the ark.
I had the opportunity in my constituency at one time to lock horns with a rather big American concern. I am not suggesting that any foreign controlled firm investing in Canada is icing on the cake or is all sweetness and light as well as a very good neighbour. That is not the case. I can recall very vividly one U.S. company which decided to go into a small community in my constituency in the forest sector. It applied to FIRA and was denied. Its representatives came to me and asked if I would assist them, and I did so. When they applied again, they were successful. If I had the opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to deny that application today, I would deny it because they lied to me and did not employ one single worker. That is the exception and we are watching those exceptions.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to welcome the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Brisco) to the House and reply to him as well. He said that we in the NDP were the shrill voice of nationalism. I

January 22, 1985
Investment Canada Act
would invite him to read the works of the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker. I think he was a Conservative and he used to speak about the values of being a Canadian, how proud he was to be a Canadian and how hard we had to fight to keep an independent Canada. I hope he would not call that being shrill. He was a Progressive Conservative of the old school of which we would like to see more in this new group of Conservatives who have become virtually Mr. Reagan's poodle. He takes them out for a walk occasionally when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) meets him in Washington or speaks in New York.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member misunderstands what FIRA was trying to do. We do not want to reduce the lifestyles of Canadians, not like the conservative Social Credit Government of British Columbia. That is reducing the lifestyles of Canadians. Poverty goes up and you get 15 per cent unemployment. We had that kind of radical restraint, that kind of policy which would open up to foreign investment, except that foreign investment did not arrive. Well, that is not the kind of policy we want to see.
Let me put to you the Conservative position as I understand it. It is that Canada needs foreign investment, but that FIRA is a hostile symbol to that investment. Because of that we are not getting our proper share of foreign investment, therefore we are not getting enough jobs. That, it seems to me, is what the argument is. I think that is superficially seductive in the sense that you want to say, yes, we want the jobs so let us open up to foreign investment. But we have to remember that we are a small country next door to a huge neighbour, but a neighbour we like very much, let us make no mistake about that. They are our allies and friends. The fact is, however, as Tommy Douglas used to say, that the elephant dances among the chickens and says: All right, boys, it is everyone for himself. There is a huge country there and we are much smaller and we have to consider that. There are costs as well as benefits to foreign investment. We would be stupid if we did not face that fact.
The reality, Mr. Speaker, is that FIRA asks a number of questions regarding foreign investment or takeovers. It says that the company coming into Canada has to show significant benefits to Canada. It sets out 10 tests. Will it provide jobs for Canadians? Will it improve Canada's export performance? Will it contribute to having more of Canada's raw materials processed within our own borders? Will the application provide new investment within Canada? Will the applicant buy supplies in Canada, provided they are competitively priced? Will there be new opportunities for Canadians to become shareholders, directors and managers of that enterprise? Will it improve Canada's access to new products and processes? Will it improve Canada's industrial productivity? Will it increase the level of competition? And is it compatible with the Government's industrial and economic policies?
Surely Conservative Members, and especially the Member who last spoke, cannot object to those kinds of tests. Surely
those are reasonable tests to protect Canadians against some of the problems and costs of foreign investment. There have been lots of studies done on this. We know that American branch plant companies tend to go home to buy their materials from their parent plant. They buy a lot more of their raw materials from the home company abroad instead of buying them in Canada.
There have been studies done by the Conservative Party's own task force on technological change which show that foreign companies tend to have their research and development done abroad. We know that is a problem. I think all rational Members, which almost all of the Members in the House are, can agree that that is a problem. We know that they tend to repatriate profits more than Canadian companies do. I am the energy critic for my Party and I have found that Canadian industry in the energy area will invest more in Canada than do the foreign multinationals. I invite you to ask Bob Blair of Nova Corporation, a Canadian businessman, who will tell you the same thing.
In other countries investment is screened. Do you know what they call FIRA in the United States? They have an agency which they call the American Congress. At this moment while we are debating, an American congressional committee is holding hearings on the objections from some American politicians and businesses to the fact that Canada has too great a share in the gas industry. We have a 6 per cent share of the gas industry in the United States. They have this continuing FIRA. Other countries have the same thing. We are not a country that is out of step because of our having an organization to consider or screen foreign investment.
The Hon. Member gave an example of a car wash in Windsor with a $4,000 investment which Cabinet has to consider. That is terrible. Let's get rid of it. Let us reform FIRA, but let us not throw it out. Let us not go further by letting the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) have the final say in certain applications. I think that would be a mistake. It seems to me that the worst of all possible worlds this country could have is what the Conservative Party may be aiming for, that is, free trade with a branch plant economy. That is the absolute worst because in the long run that will mean a decline in jobs and in the economy of Canada.
We could end up with an economy with an even higher degree of foreign ownership than at present and a diminished capacity to export and innovate and, hence, to make our own way in an increasingly competitive world. Therefore, in the long run, passing this legislation and getting rid of FIRA rather than reforming it could result in fewer rather than more jobs for Canadians.
An editorial in the Toronto Star dated December 9, 1984 reads as follows:
The agency's greatest role, indeed, has not been in screening out foreign investment, but in acting as a bargaining lever to persuade would-be investors to sweeten the pot in terms of providing more jobs and benefits for Canadians.
It is the Conservatives who are being ideological here. They are living in a world that is not real. They are being shrill and
January 22, 1985

selling out the Canadian worker in the long run. It is a seductive argument for people, especially in these bad economic times, but we need an agency such as other countries have which will in fact screen foreign investment, rather than throw it out, and make sure that there are significant benefits to Canada. Only in that way can we have an economy that really works.
That is why we in this Party support the amendment to hoist this Bill for six months so that the Government can come back with some decent legislation which will protect us from the costs of foreign investment, rather than just taking this kind of Pollyanna look at the benefits which are supposed to result.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate for a few minutes in this debate on Bill C-15 to create Investment Canada. What I will attempt to do briefly is to show that the intended purpose of the present debate is to score political points rather than attracting the foreign investment we need in Canada.
First of all, it must be said that we do need investments from abroad. Everyone in Canada complains about the fact that there are 1.5 million unemployed. We have vast natural resources, qualified workers who are willing and eager to work and many of whom cannot find a job. We therefore all agree on the general objective of attracting foreign investment. However, I must point out immediately that there are two risks involved. The first is that most of this foreign investment would come from the same country, which has sometimes been the case in the past, thus leaving Canadians wide open to damaging consequences should this foreign country, which has invested massively in Canada, brings about legislative changes detrimental to our interests. Another danger, of course, would be to let foreign interests invest in all areas of Canadian activity without bothering about the fact that some of these areas must be protected in the interests of all Canadians. I am thinking of areas such as finance. As Canadians, we certainly do not want foreign interests to control our financial institutions. At the same time, there is the cultural danger that foreign investors might take over our medias, our publications, or our radio and television stations.
What I wish to emphasize is that, while doing everything in its power to attract investments from abroad, the previous Liberal Government had provided adequate safeguards to protect us from the first danger namely that, to a large extent, the investments would come from the same country. We can recall the initiative of Mr. Trudeau who had tried to provide an alternative by personally approaching European countries in an effort to attract investments from that part of the world. I repeat that the danger would be that most investments might be made by the same country. In this regard, everyone knows that I am thinking about our neighbours to the South.
The attempt to diversify investments from abroad was a laudable effort on the part of the previous government. There
Investment Canada Act
is nothing in the present attitude of the Progressive Conservatives to show that they are trying to diversify our foreign investments. On the contrary, their whole public relations operation consists of going down on their knees before the American giant, before Uncle Sam, and of begging our neighbours to invest in Canada. For our part, we certainly want American investments, but we also want investments from Japan, from Germany, from France, from Australia and from most other industrialized countries. The record clearly shows that, in the past, we took action to try to diversify the source of foreign investments in Canada, but the same cannot be said about the present government which is trying something rather strange. Its rhetoric aims at attracting investments by suggesting that the previous government wanted to prevent and reject foreign investments. Of course, this is ridiculous.
Another message that the Progressive Conservative Government is trying to convey is that the Foreign Investment Review Agency, FIRA as it is called in English and sometimes even in French, systematically turned down most foreign investors and blocked the influx of foreign capitals. Nothing could be further from the truth! If we look at the decisions made by FIRA, we realize that, at the most, about 3 per cent of applications were rejected. It is therefore spurious to blame the Liberal Party of Canada for having created FIRA and to say that by doing so it prevented foreign capital from entering Canada.
Quite the opposite, I would suggest that over the last two or three years, the repeated attacks by the Progressive Conservative Party in the House of Commons, and outside the House in the media, their constant criticism of FIRA has scared away foreign investors because of their unrelented allegations suggesting that it was hard to get capital into Canada because with FIRA the Liberals were blocking the entry of capital. Well, with 3 per cent only of past applications being refused, it is readily obvious that all this is pure rhetoric. It is a public relations game designed to have Canadians believe that the Conservatives have such an insight into the economy, that they are so much more eager than we Liberals are to get foreign capital, which of course is an outright invention.
Be that as it may, I look forward to hearing details of how this Government will go about ensuring that foreign investments coming into Canada will not jeopardize certain particular Canadian interests, especially in the cultural and the financial fields I was referring to earlier.
The Government has already suggested that it was going to closely monitor those fields in order to protect them from foreign control. But in saying this, the Conservative Government is actually endorsing the Liberal policy under which FIRA, the screening agency, was established specifically to pursue those goals.
So please let us put an end to all this rhetoric here. Let us stop accusing one another. It is my view that all parties in this House are in agreement as to the importance for Canada of investments coming from abroad and from south of the border,

January 22, 1985
Investment Canada Act
to develop our resources and create the jobs that are in such dire need.
In any case, as far as the Liberal Party of Canada, the Official Opposition, is concerned, let it be clear that we support foreign investments in Canada, let nobody fall for our opponents rhetoric, which would have people believe that we are opposing foreign investment.
As well, we want these foreign investments to be diversified and to come from several countries rather than one country. We do not want to be at the mercy of legislation passed south of the border that could be detrimental to us. We advocate more investment but from more countries. That is the policy of the Liberal Party of Canada.

Therefore, let us stop accusing one another. And as the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) who spoke before me has suggested that Bill C-15 was superficially appealing, I would suggest for my part that it is a rather superficial piece of legislation. Indeed, this is the reason why my party has introduced a motion to postpone discussion on this Bill, to give the Government a chance to review the problems that must be solved if we want Canada to attract more foreign investments, and especially to make sure that such investments will be in the interest of Canadians. No doubt that some reflection will help the Government introduce a more comprehensive piece of legislation, reconsider its rhetoric and realize that we will not attract foreign capital just by criticizing the previous government.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this assembly today for the first time to comment on the legislation which plans the creation of Investment Canada, as it is somewhat speculatively called, and on the motion to hoist this legislation for a six-month period. In doing so, since this is my first speech in the House of Commons, I should like to take the opportunity to comment on my constituency and on several aspects of the parliamentary process that I feel are worthy of being on the public record.
Let me commence by paying tribute to my immediate predecessor, the Hon. John Reid, who represented Kenora-Rainy River for a period of over 17 years and whom I, eventually and at the third try, replaced here. One of my colleagues charitably says "third time lucky", but he knows as well as I do that luck is when preparation meets opportunity. It is that preparation upon which I will comment later.
Mr. Reid served his riding well, according to his lights and principles and certainly for a long time. He said that he had spent more than half of his adult life in this Chamber and that now he has the opportunity to spend his time in other pursuits.
I should like to pay tribute to his predecessor, the late Senator William Benidickson, who passed away a matter of
days ago and is survived by a very devoted and great lady, his wife Agnes. Mr. Benidickson served in this Chamber for nigh on 20 years and as a Cabinet Minister in several posts. He also had a great commitment to democracy, a great commitment to his legal profession and to the people of the Kenora-Rainy River riding.
For me it is an historic day in that this is the first time that a Member for Kenora-Rainy River has ever risen in the House from a seat any place other than on the benches of the Liberal Party. I stand to be corrected, but it may be that the campaign team that put me in this place broke the longest winning streak in Canadian political history.
The riding of Kenora-Rainy River is among the five largest in the country. It is the size of both Germanys put together. It has a population of nearly 80,000, which is spread out in an average density of one for every four square kilometres. For those of us who are not bilingual or bicultural, it is something less than one person for every square mile. They have a diversity of occupations which is truly incredible. It ranges from farmers to trappers, hunters, pilots, miners, lumberjacks and factory, plant, mill and railroad workers. There are many who are employed in the service of either the federal or provincial Governments and many who, like myself before coming to this place, were private businessmen or professionals in private practice.
I dare say that, with over 100 communities in an area the size of Germany, mine is one of the most diversified ridings represented in this Chamber and possibly also one of the hardest to represent.
During our recess-referred to so often and so inaccurately by journalists as a vacation-I personally travelled well over 5,000 miles in the service of my constituents. That is besides a two-week vacation during which I also travelled.
I should like to comment briefly on the ethnic background and make-up of my constituency. Most of this part of Canada was formally ceded to the Crown, formally recognized the sovereignty of the Crown, as late as 1929, 1930 and 1931. There are people alive today who remember the time when a large part of my riding was not part of Canada but was the sovereign territory of the Anishinabek, whose descendants still occupy it today.
It is a great privilege for me to represent the Anishinabek. Napich keechee-enandan kai-seck che-a-anee to-mou-ka anishinabek. I am grateful to them for their strong support. Ga-chee-enan-dan ka-ke wee-chee (ka-pou-tou) show-watch. [Translation]
I also consider it a privilege to represent people of various linguistic groups, the Francophones in my constituency and people of Ukranian, German, Dutch, and Polish origin, people from every European nation probably, from most nations in the world that are represented either by immigrants or descendants.

I think it would also be appropriate for me to tell the House today that I am a new Canadian myself. The general election which saw me elected to this Chamber was called on the fourteenth anniversary of my arrival in Canada. That day, of course, will always stay in my memory. One of my favourite themes when I have the opportunity and the privilege to address a gathering, be it in my riding or anywhere else, is the degree of opportunity that is available to us in Canada today. I cannot conceive of having the sort of opportunities I have had in Canada had I elected to remain in my own country. I tell my friends, and it is only partially in jest, that I am a refugee from English beer, from tea, and from Toryism.
Oh, oh!

There would be those who would say that I have got my come-uppance. I have managed to avoid both tea and English beer. It seems that Toryism, and I must say this with some regret, has a certain air of inescapability about it, particularly in this Chamber. I would say to my friends opposite, and I would caution them very strongly, not to take it too much to heart because there are, after all, those among them who differ. Let me say that I would much rather be sitting across from them even with their swollen numbers than across from the Tories who presently rule my native country and who are so busily engaged in wreaking destruction upon that country's economy, trade, and social fabric, a destruction which I trust my friends across the way not to repeat in this our Canada.
Hear, hear!

I would not be here today, Mr. Speaker, without the support of my Party, without the support of my many personal friends and political friends in the Kenora-Rainy River riding, and particularly not without the support of my wife and family. I shall always acknowledge that support and will always be grateful for it. It will always stand in my mind as one of the great thrills of my life.
As I said before, Kenora-Rainy River is made up of over 100 communities ranging from tiny villages of less than 100 people to the prosperous bustling communities of up to 10,000 people in the case of Kenora. It includes such mill towns as Dryden and Fort Frances, railroad and government communities such as Sioux Lookout, and mining towns such as Ear Falls and Red Lake.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Government House Leader and his colleagues for extending that courtesy and civility-
And our friends to the right.

And our friends to the right, as I am reminded by my colleagues, for extending that courtesy and civility for which I am sure in time he will become universally renowned.
I was embarking on a comparison of my constituency with many others in this country. While I feel they are not more favoured, more blessed or more richly endowed, they are in many ways more privileged. But I will stay those remarks for another day and perhaps will briefly conclude with some remarks on the subject matter of this motion and the Bill before us.
We are familiar with the various analogies that have been used to describe our state of economic affairs as compared with those of our neighbour to the south. I recall one person who was long in this place, although he never demonstrated great respect for it, saying that the Canadian situation was similar to that of a mouse sleeping beside an elephant. It would appear from some of the public statements and also the privately expressed views of our neighbours to the south that we are sometimes seen as the Fifty-First state. It is perhaps fortunate, but in other ways unfortunate, that we are part of a continental economy whether we like it or not and that whatever barriers we erect in the way of that continental economy, or indeed whatever paths we smooth the trade that exists between our country and the United States of America is like an umbilical cord. It provides nourishment. However, from our perspective, it works north to south rather than south to north. There the analogy to our co-operation with this economic giant ends.
I should like to dwell on the difference between investment and purchase and to say that what is investment from the point of view of the investor is not necessarily investment from the point of view of a country in which the investment is made. When a Canadian business is purchased, the investment should surely be judged, not by the price paid nor by the change of control of the corporate structure that is used to effect such investment, but on what accrues to Canada as a result of that purchase or change of control. Investments are only made, in the strictest sense of the word, when new productive assets are put in place such that there will be benefits not only to the person making the investment but also

January 22, 1985
Adjournment Motion
to the community or country and, yes, to the workers in the plant or establishment in which that investment occurs.
We have seen in our country the use of foreign investment to further our development. We have also seen the degree to which foreign investment has meant a repatriation of profits. We have seen a patriation from Canada to the United States of the engineering and research and development components of the company or enterprise that has been taken over. We have seen Canada used as surplus capacity because of such investments. We have seen decisions taken that will not be in the economic interests of Canada, Canadians or the communities affected.
We cannot afford to let Investment Canada be perceived as fire sale Canada. The coincidence between the establishment of this agency and the Government's expressed intention to sell off any Crown corporations for which it can find buyers is surely a little too compelling, particularly in the minds of the observers, those who have the cash and the capital and who might make investments. Therefore, I call upon the House to support this motion and to delay for a six-month period consideration of Bill C-15.
Hear, hear!
