speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate on the amendment proposed by my colleague from Windsor West (Mr. Gray), namely that Bill C-15 be not now read a second time but be read a second time six months hence. As you know, Mr. Speaker, we proposed this amendment to give all Members of this House a chance to speak to this very important legislation, Bill C-15. No great feats of imagination are necessary to find clear-cut examples of foreign takeovers in Canadian industry, business and the economy in every riding and every region in our country, and the reason this screening agency was proposed a number of years ago was to strengthen our Canadian economy, not only for its own sake but also to safeguard jobs and, by promoting research and development, to create more economic activity that would produce more jobs.
We are not the only country in the world to set up a screening agency. The Americans have their own procedures and Japan and several other countries have government agencies that are supposed to control foreign takeovers. In the United States, foreign companies may not control companies in certain economic sectors including marine transportation, broadcasting, air transportation and defence production. It is absolutely impossible for a foreign country or corporation to take control of such industries. Australia, for instance, has a Foreign Investment Review Board very similar to our own and Japan exercises very extensive control over foreign investment.
This kind of measure is not out of the ordinary, in that it is already being used in many countries to screen investment.
Mr. Speaker, according to a number of observers, this Bill more or less proposes to open wide the doors of this country to foreign investment, which obviously implies foreign control over very significant economic sectors, whether industrial, commercial or other. I am thinking of a few examples in my own riding of Ottawa-Vanier, which is not an industrial riding, since it has a high percentage of professionals and public servants who are employed by the Government to indeed serve the public. The largest employer in my riding is the University of Ottawa, which has 3,000 employees in Ottawa-Vanier.
Two years ago, the University was having serious problems with its bookstore. Sales were declining, administration costs were very high, and the bookstore was losing between $100,-
January 22, 1985

000 and $200,000 per year. No rent was charged and the bookstore was perpetually in the red. The University looked for ways to get the bookstore out of the red. Canadian industry, including both publishers and distributors, showed an interest. An American company, Brennan College Service Inc., also became interested and made the University an offer. Negotiations, which lasted nearly a year, made it clear that it was not in Canada's interests to let an American company take over this bookstore and thus, according to some people, become a threat to the Canadian book industry and professional and academic publishing.
FIRA examined and rejected an initial application by Brennan College Service Inc., for the simple reason that it did not meet FIRA's requirement for generating significant benefits for Canada. This is a very important point: significant benefits for Canada, which means there seemed to be nothing to justify a foreign takeover. Following FIRA's refusal, the administration of the University of Ottawa signed a new agreement with the American company under which the University would retain ownership of the bookstore and Brennan College Service Inc. would work with the University on restructuring the bookstore which, as I said before, was in the red.
I was speaking yesterday to the Vice-Rector for Administration who said that things were going well, that the Canadian company, Ottawa Brennan Inc., was operating satisfactorily, that everything seemed to indicate that they would make a profit of around $100,000 this year and that the University of Ottawa was very pleased to have a foreign company as the minority interest within a Canadian company. I have nothing against foreign technology if it can help us acquire new expertise, in administration or manpower training, for instance. In fact, the Vice-Rector of the University commented that they were able to take advantage of the expertise of Brennan College Service Inc. and training provided by the company for employees of the University of Ottawa Bookstore. The outcome was very fortunate, since in the process, an American company was prevented from taking full control of a business in my riding of Ottawa-Vanier, and also the business was able to continue, because I think that otherwise, the University would have been forced to close down the bookstore. So it was a fortunate experience, but it was FIRA's final decision which helped to bring about this agreement. So that was my experience during the past two years with the federal Government's Foreign Investment Review Agency, and I must say it was very worthwhile.
Without FIRA, the University of Ottawa Bookstore would probably have gone out of business and become U.S.-owned. Many people, including myself, feel that the American company does not have the cultural expertise and the biculturalism of the University of Ottawa, nor the University's bilingual capacity. This was not part of the company's makeup, and we might have lost some of that respect for both languages we have been trying to build up as well as the positive attitude to
Investment Canada Act
the many cultures thriving in our community. I therefore feel this was a very fortunate solution to a rather serious problem.
This government has introduced Bill C-15, Investment Canada, which provides that 90 per cent of proposed acquisitions of Canadian small and medium-size companies will not even be subject to review by the Investment Canada agency.
Given such a Bill, how can we possibly expect to meet our long-sought challenge-to have a Canadian product patterned after Canadians?
Before establishing its trade strategy, Canada must be in a position to control its economic base. If that base belongs to foreign interests, Canada's decision-making power on the international scene will be severely limited. The government was not given a mandate to make Canada lose its national identity. Canadians love their country, they are friendly people in the widest and deepest meaning of the word, but they are not the kind of people who would sell out their national identity simply to cut a striking figure before the United States.
The government must have misunderstood its mandate. Recent economic history shows clearly that, in times of recession and various crises, the interests of creditor countries take precedence over those of debtor countries. Foreign takeovers can also lead to lost national identity, particularly when sensitive sectors such as education and culture are involved.
Earlier, Mr. Speaker, I was talking about education. I see that you are about to rise to interrupt me. Perhaps I will have another opportunity to speak to the House on that issue. I respect your ruling and close my remarks.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate with some regret about the Bill we are debating. What we have in front of us is only more cosmetics and superficiality. I see nothing in the contents of this Bill that will advance the cause of job creation anywhere in the country. The Bill provides more of the smoke and mirrors that we have become accustomed to over the past several months.
The implication is given that by changing the name of FIRA and by making other superficial changes, somehow investment from the United States will suddenly speed up. The implication is also that this did not happen before. That is a myth that we should put to rest right away.
Anybody who cares to research The Globe and Mail- FIRA applications were all published the day after they were approved by Cabinet-will see laid out very clearly that over 90 per cent, the vast majority, of applications that came before FIRA and Cabinet were approved. It is a myth to say that somehow there was a bottleneck or stoppage of applications from the U.S. or any foreign country. That is a myth that
1570

January 22, 1985
Investment Canada Act
should be laid to rest right away. This is one reason why the Bill is superficial.
The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) used that application, and he was right. It is wrong to tell people through this Bill that suddenly, if you make those changes and call the corporation Investment Canada and stop calling it FIRA, with those cosmetic changes U.S. investment will flow. It will not happen as simply as that. U.S. analysts have said publicly that by doing that, it ain't going to change overnight.
Investment in the United States, even within that country, is moving from the northeast to the southwest. They have a problem within their country of declining industries and declining areas. New industries are taking over and they are attracting investment. Even within the United States that kind of situation is taking place. To suggest that because you introduce this Bill and change the name U.S. investment will flow over the border is not correct. It is not as simple as that.
What the Government should be putting before us instead of this Bill is ways and means to encourage the right type of industry in the various regions of Canada. We have Silicon Valley in California and we have silicon valley right here in the National Capital Region. What we should have before us instead of these cosmetics is a strategy whereby new futuristic industries can be encouraged in the regions of the country. That is what the Government should be putting in front of us. How can we attract more high tech firms to the Atlantic area and to various areas in western Canada? That is the kind of policy I would like to see the Government put forward instead of these cosmetics.
Whatever happened to a regional development policy? When is the Government going to tell us how it intends to build up the regions of this country? Certainly we have not seen those measures so far. I would like the Government very soon to spell out very clearly its policy on regional development. When this Party was in power, there was a key element of our policy devoted to regional economic development, but I have not heard that mentioned. I have seen the negative effects of the cut-backs that have been put in place. We have not seen that U.S. investment until now.
The fact is that apart from keeping out U.S. investment, we have been trying to encourage it. When we created Fishery Products International in Newfoundland, many people tried to get private sector investment for that company wherever it was available. All of us, no matter what side of the House we are on, agree that only through private sector investment are we going to create long-term jobs. That did not come and Governments had to step in and provide the capital that was needed.
Another industry will be familiar, namely, the iron ore industry. Apart from attracting new American capital, we are seeing the Americans pull out capital and emphasize operations other than those which they hold in Canada. The Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway made that point very clearly, and he was right. Just because you have an American branch plant in your country does not mean that you have a secure future. In fact, the opposite may be true. Let us not fool
ourselves that by attracting American capital we are automatically going to be on easy street. The fact is that they have been looking after their own interests first and ours second. We should be very wary of that.
We have no hesitation, certainly in my province, about having American capital. We have had a long, warm relationship with the Americans. I remember my grandfather sailing to New England in the days of sail when it was known in my province as the Boston States. We have a very lucrative trade with the eastern United States. Atlantic Canada still does, as we do on the West Coast and in the areas represented by Members all over this Chamber. They have a very healthy trade, particularly the border provinces, with the U.S.
At the time of Confederation in 1949 when we joined Canada, one of the options put before the people of Newfoundland by Don Jamieson, a former colleague in this Chamber who is now elsewhere, was economic union with the United States. Throughout World War II we had five important bases in my province. Many American servicemen in Newfoundland married Newfoundland girls who then went to live in the United States. The real reason for the boom in the economy in the United States at the present time is not Reaganomics. It is all those Newfoundland girls who married American servicemen and created the new Americans who are adding to the vitality of that country at this time.
We have no hesitation in welcoming the Americans with open arms. We have been friends of theirs for decades, indeed centuries. Let us not kid ourselves that they are somehow the enemy at our gates that we have to keep out. They are not. We want and need that investment. That is the only way to create long-term jobs. However, it cannot be done through cosmetics and superficialities. We must come forward with something with more substance than that.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to plug something here. It is a bit of a black market operation and a bit of a subterfuge. However, let me say that one of the reasons given for the screening of investments being processed through the new Investment Canada is the protection of the Canadian cultural heritage. That seems to be all right on the surface of it. There is nothing wrong with being in favour of the Canadian cultural heritage. However, let us not let the Government encourage it on the one hand and discourage it on the other. The Government cannot say that it will screen investments through a Bill like this for possible detraction from the Canadian cultural heritage while at the same time making cut-backs to the CBC.
If something is damaging the cultural heritage of the country, it is the closing and downgrading of various CBC stations, and particularly those in small, remote communities in northern Canada. The only voice, mirror or self-image that those people have is their local CBC station. Now when many communities are fighting for survival, the very means of protecting their self-image and indeed their cultural heritage is being taken away from them. I would ask the Government to
January 22, 1985

review that policy and to intervene with the CBC in order to see that those stations that we need so badly for the protection of our cultural heritage are not taken away from us.
I can give as an example of this the station in Labrador City which is in a remote area formerly served by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) when he was President of the Iron Ore Company of Canada. Communities such as that one are fighting for their lives at the present time. As we know, the iron ore and steel industries are struggling for survival. I do not believe that they are sunset industries by any stretch of the imagination, but they are going through some very rough times. Now, when they are struggling for survival, it seems to me that it is wrong to take away their voice, their self-image and the protection of their cultural heritage. I do not believe that the Government can, on the one hand, say that it can protect this and, on the other hand, take steps to destroy it. If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would ask government Members to review that policy.
I am afraid that what we have before us at the present time is nothing of substance but more fluff and more cosmetics from a Government that has certainly become known for that in the economic fields. Perhaps government Members need time. I know that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has put forward policy statements which have some substance. We may agree or disagree with these statements, but at least there is some substance to them. The same thing must happen in terms of economic policy.
The Government must put before us meaningful measures for job creation. Instead, what we have are cut-backs. For example, there have been cut-backs in unemployment insurance at a time when job creation is at an all-time high in my own province. For example, there have been cut-backs in the fisheries infrastructure at a time when that particular industry is struggling for survival. There have been increases in the ferry rates to Newfoundland. Ferries are the very lifeline of islands like mine and Prince Edward Island. If the ferry rates are increased, not only will it discourage business and add to its costs but an added burden will be put on the consumer who has the least ability to bear that burden.
Instead of receiving meaningful job-creation measures, we have received cut-backs which will have a negative effect on our economy. I say to the Government that now is the time to forget the posturing, the rhetoric and the public relations and get on with putting before us real policies for meaningful job creation in the country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in my place today and take this opportunity to address this Bill. I find that I must rise today to caution against what seems to be the unbridled enthusiasm of the Government for advertising Canada as being open for business with no strings attached. I of course have no complaint with the notion that Canada is open for business. I applaud any initiative that brings legitimate investment capital into the country. I remind the Government that approximately 97 per cent of the applications that were brought before FIRA in the past year were approved in any case. Simply changing
Investment Canada Act
the name of this agency from FIRA to Investment Canada, while it is a lovely cosmetic change, will not in and of itself have much impact on job creation in the country.
At the very time that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is telling Canadians and the assembled group of boardroom chairmen from the United States that Canada is open for business, there are certain groups in the United States telling us that the United States may not be open to Canadian exports. Canadians know that a few friendly words which passed between the President and the Prime Minister in March do not mean influence over the administration, much less over Congress or various sectors of the U.S. economy. In particular, I speak of the softwood lumber industry for which efforts have been renewed in the last few weeks to curb Canadian exports.
Canada is by far the world's largest exporter of lumber. We supply over 40 per cent of the world's total supply of lumber. More than 66 per cent of those exports from Canada went to the United States in 1982. Of that amount, 56 per cent came from the Province of British Columbia alone.
It seems to me to be somewhat frightening that, on the one hand, while we are advertising that Canada is open for business and has been open for business for some time, on the other hand the United States has increased protectionist tendencies. The softwood lumber sector in the United States is moving rapidly not by means of protest but, in its own mind, by means of legislation to prohibit or restrict to a minimal amount the importation of lumber from Canada.
The forestry industry is the single largest producer and generator of jobs in this country. There is no bigger industry. In terms of our balance of trade, it is bigger than agriculture, fisheries, mining and oil and gas all put together. That is how critical this industry is to Canada. Unfortunately, in the House of Commons and, I would suggest, across the country among the public at large and in particular in the Cabinet, there is not much appreciation of that very real and very startling simple economic statistic.
Rather than getting on with the business of making cosmetic changes to the names of agencies, rather than managing by media manipulation, rather than tying its appearance of competence to the ability of its media managers, I would like to ask the Government when, in addition to practising its love-in with the current United States administration, it will stand up and defend Canadian interests. This administration recently signed an agreement restricting Canadian shipments of duty-free newsprint into Europe to 600,000 tonnes annually. Our quota used to be 1.5 million tonnes annually. I have just told the House about the importance of softwood lumber. Let me tell Hon. Members as well that newsprint is the second major component in the value of the Canadian forestry industry. Over 100 communities in Canada are single-industry towns which are dependent on this industry. Yet an agreement was signed during the Christmas recess, the details of which were announced on December 27 when nobody was paying attention. That agreement restricts Canada's ability to go duty-free into that market. An industry spokesman in The

January 22, 1985
Investment Canada Act
Chronicle-Herald of Halifax a few days ago described it as an unfair decision which was reached without any consultation with industry representatives. If the industry was not consulted, can we assume that other Canadians were consulted?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The industry was consulted.

I would say to the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) that The Chronicle-Herald indicated that the industry was not consulted and has described the decision as "an unfair decision". Where is the commitment for consultation that the Government promised? I should point out that the agreement was rejected by the previous administration. The previous administration refused to sign it and saw it as being basically unfair. The previous administration recognized-if we understand the growth that will occur in this sector by the year 2000-that it would foreclose in advance Canada's job creation opportunities for the future. The previous administration turned it down, but this administration signed it and announced its decision on December 27. What was it trying to hide?
Some time ago I suggested to the Prime Minister that he would do himself and the country a great service if he would bring with him into the House a set of ear-plugs. The House has had the unfortunate spectacle of a Prime Minister who has misunderstood the applause of 211 cheering and, with all due respect, mindless supporters, and has taken that applause as being the approval of the people of Canada for the policies which are being announced. I want to tell the Prime Minister that, if he has misunderstood the applause of his tribe for the approval of the people of Canada, he ought to go out with his Secretary of State for External Affairs and his Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) and consult the people in the forest industry about the agreement which was signed with the EEC that will foreclose Canada's future possibilities for growth in that industry. He ought to find out how people in the lumber industry feel about the renewed threat of a limitation on Canadian exports into the U.S. But we have not heard a peep out of the administration.
When I see a Government which has been in power for four months and has not put forward one piece of original or substantial legislation, and which wastes the time of the House by changing the name of FIRA to Investment Canada, I am reminded a bit of the little old lady in the Wendy's commercial. The people of Canada have sent 211 sets of buns to the House. I want to ask, "Where the hell is the beef?"
May I humbly suggest that a six-month hoist is appropriate and is in order at this time.
You have never been humble in your life.

I would suggest to the administration that when it has some beef and some measures of meaty substance to bring before the House for our humble consideration, it should attempt once again to attract the undivided and serious attention of this humble House.

Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to rise today to discuss a motion to delay the implementation of the Investment Canada Bill for six months for further study. It is an excellent and necessary amendment.
The Government is proposing to protect the cultural heritage of Canada, and government Members have stated during the course of the debate that that is why the Government is not permitting foreign investment in the areas which it deems to be cultural-broadcasting, newspapers and the like. However, one of the arguments which we have made on this side of the House is that a cultural heritage cannot be protected by allowing the economy to be controlled by outside forces. I will not spend much time arguing that point, except to point out something of which we are all very aware, which is that in Canada the cultural heritage of our native people was not very well protected once their economy was taken away from them. I submit that there will be no cultural heritage for Canada if the Canadian economy is gradually eroded, taken away from us and allowed to fall into foreign hands.
I believe good use could be made of the six months to study further the implications of the Bill. I have identified seven problems in the approach which the Government has taken. The Government is assuming that if it attracts foreigners, business will develop and jobs will be created. I have a great deal of difficulty with that, because Canada has been following that line of reasoning since the Second World War, with only the minor change of the establishment of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. The problems are numerous, but I will only outline seven problems which are evident in the legislation.
The first problem is that foreign companies do not spend nearly as much on research and development as do Canadian-controlled companies. Research and development is a key source of economic growth and productivity in our economy. Yet, if we look at the track record of Canadian firms versus foreign-controlled firms, we find that Canadian firms have a much better record of performing research and development than do foreign firms. I would refer the House to two studies, one which was done by the Economic Council of Canada in 1983 and another which was done by the Science Council of Canada in 1984. Both of those studies had similar results. They found that Canadian firms with less than 50 employees spent about 11.2 per cent of their sales in research and development, whereas an operation of the same size which was owned by foreign interests only reinvested 3.3 per cent of its sales.
The studies present a long table which I will not go into, but the proportions get worse as the companies get larger. Canadian-controlled companies with more than 500 employees invested 10.3 per cent of their sales in research and development, while foreign-owned companies reinvested a paltry 2 per cent. Research and development ensures long-term jobs. I submit, on the basis of the findings of the Economic Council and the Science Council-and each organization performed separate research and had results which were very much the same- that foreign firms do not do a good job in R and D. Subse-

quently, they will not produce as many jobs as Canadian-owned firms.
The second problem that is evident with the concept the Conservatives are pursuing is that foreign-controlled firms import much more than Canadian-controlled firms. Again, I have some numbers that I would like to put on the record which indicate that the spinoff benefits which would accrue from purchases from Canadian companies, mostly inside the country, which create other jobs subsequent to the original purchase, do not accrue when the company doing the purchasing is a foreign-owned company making its purchases from head office in the home country. In fact, foreign companies imported 22 per cent of their sales, which is five times the amount imported by Canadian companies. Of the companies which are involved in manufacturing, foreign companies imported 30 per cent of their sales, which is four times the amount imported by Canadian companies.
It is evident from these figures that foreign companies have a predilection to import from the country of their origin and do not provide the necessary multiplier effect to keep the Canadian economy growing and to prepare the way for jobs to be created in Canada.
The third problem we have with the move to more foreign control of our economy is that foreign-controlled firms make a higher proportion of payments outside of the country. I am speaking now of interest and dividend payments and service charges payable to the head office. This reduces the resources available to Canada, and reduces the opportunity for more jobs and more investment resulting from those profits. As an example, American-controlled firms holding 36 per cent of the industrial assets in Canada in 1981, accounted for 61 per cent of all external remittances. So you can see that, compared to Canadian firms, they exported capital at the rate of two to one. Foreign-owned firms do not have a record nearly as good as the Canadian-owned operations and are not as useful in recycling money and creating jobs in Canada. In fact, they exacerbate the problem by creating a large wound in the economic body of the country which drains money outside of the country.
A fourth problem which I would like to deal with today is that multinational corporations seek to maximize global profits by minimizing tax payments. Some of the countries in which they operate have high taxes and others have low taxes. They then do internal shifting of funds by charging various service fees so that their profits are larger in those countries with the lowest effective tax rate. As an example, a study of the computer industry found a $50 million tax loss through this mechanism, equal to an amount 30 per cent lower than what should have been paid given the amount of money actually earned in our country. That comes from a report done in 1981 by the Evans Research Corporation. I think that in the course of the next six months the House would be well advised to become acquainted with the research which shows that this
Investment Canada Act
particular policy decision the Tories have embarked upon is a hazardous one for the country.
The fifth problem we see with this approach is that foreign-controlled companies export much less real product in relation to sales than do their Canadian competitors. In fact, some studies indicate, as the Gray report did, that 90 per cent of the exports of Canadian subsidiaries went to U.S. parents in 1978, when the report was completed, and that 57 per cent of U.S. subsidiaries restricted exports from their Canadian plants. The head office makes certain that the home country gets the advantage of having that subsidiary in a foreign country, in this case Canada, and that the country being colonized, if you like, gets very minimal benefits.
To go quickly to the sixth problem, Mr. Speaker, a high ratio of foreign control of Canadian industry contributes to poor productivity performance by reducing competition, a conclusion that the Science Council found as recently as 1984.
I would conclude by noting that studies by the U.S. Senate and the Harvard School of Business have found that U.S. direct investment in Canada produces a significant net creation of jobs for all sectors of the U.S. workforce but for Canada, the other side of the coin, there is a net loss of jobs. I think that makes the point, Mr. Speaker, and I will now allow another Member to speak.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in favour of the motion to hoist the Bill and delay its consideration for at least six months. I think this makes sense because, once again the new government has got caught up in its own rhetoric. It believes so much in the free enterprise principle that it cannot fully appreciate the impact of this legislation.
There are two elements in what I guess will probably be a two-part presentation, Mr. Speaker. I would like to deal with how they affect my region of northwestern Ontario. We are at the western end of Ontario and we probably think of ourselves more as part of western Canada than of eastern Canada. One of the problems we have had since the area was first settled was how to attract the investment dollars we need to develop employment and the wealth that so often we miss out on. Just like western Canada, we see money being spent in the Golden Horseshoe around Toronto. Manufacturing is developed there using our resources, the raw materials taken usually from one-industry towns over a period of 20 to 30 years. Those towns are then left without any kind of secondary or tertiary industries to fall back on. In the Foreign Investment Review Agency we at least had a mechanism to try to focus, funnel or, if you like, control where investment, albeit foreign investment, could be placed. That is not to say that I agree with the manner in which FIRA was operating because I believe, and I am sure you will concur, that a government which philosophically does not believe in intervention in the marketplace has really no business intervening because it usually mucks it up. It puts on so many checks and balances to protect its interest that it is an inefficient mechanism and really does not do what it was meant to do. We saw how the Liberals dealt with FIRA in that manner.

January 22, 1985
Indian Self-Government
Without the controlling mechanism which could have been used in FIRA, and which is definitely not in Investment Canada, any foreign money invested here will go to the Golden Horseshoe area of Ontario to boost the manufacturing sector. But we in northwestern Ontario, and I suggest every other part of this country, will not get the investment we need in order to produce new wealth. It will not focus investment in a community like Atikokan, in Ear Falls, which is currently undergoing a severe employment crisis. It will not help the community of Thunder Bay which has in excess of 14,000 men and women currently seeking full-time employment. I suspect that before this winter is out that number will rise to over 15,000. Investment Canada is not going to steer money to northwestern Ontario and those communities.
I think that if we gave this government six months to do the kind of research that my colleague referred to, to rethink the Bill, perhaps instead of a weakening of our control over our own destiny, we will have a mechanism which will ensure that the money, whether it be Canadian or otherwise, will be used to benefit the Canadian public.
I will take my chair for the moment, Mr. Speaker, and resume tomorrow.

The House resumed, from December 4, 1984, consideration of the motion of Mr. Penner:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of promoting Indian self-government by:
1.	Announcing support for an affirmative policy of constitutional recognition of aboriginal self-government;
2.	Pursuing actively, a bilateral process of discussion with representatives of first nations on such issues as self-government, natives claims and the elimination of the extinguishment policy; and
3.	Introducing legislation to recognize first nations self-government which should be developed by means of a joint process and utilization of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to speak on a motion which was introduced a few weeks ago with regard to Indian self-government. When I left off my remarks a few weeks ago I had not had the opportunity to go into detail in some of the areas I feel we should be considering. Over the last number of weeks and months I have sat on the Standing Committee for Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I have been able to study in more detail what Indian Affairs is all about and what the problems of native people are. I would like to relate my remarks strictly to the riding of Timiskaming in northern Ontario. There we have bands in the Moose Factory area, the Temagami area and in the North Bay and Sturgeon Falls areas.
We as elected officials have to study the problems facing the native people of Canada. One and a half years ago the committee of this House toured Canada to deal with some of the problems affecting native people. Native housing in the area of James Bay, for example, is an area that we will be addressing. The previous Government failed over the last 16 years to deal with the tragedy which has affected the native people's livelihoods over a long period of time. The previous Government did not deal with the medical problems in the James Bay area. I am very pleased to say that this Government and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) will certainly be dealing with that. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will be in Thunder Bay tomorrow to meet with the chiefs of Treaty 9 which comprises the James Bay, lower mainland area.
This Government is trying to co-operate and work with the native people to solve the problems which have affected them over the last number of years. That is why I have a problem with dealing so quickly with this motion on Indian self-government. This Government wants to work with the native people and the provinces to resolve the problems which have been caused over the years. We will be dealing with housing problems and the health care system which have been neglected over the years.
One area that we must address very quickly is the unemployment problem of native people, whether on reserve or off reserve. Native people across the country have not been given the opportunity to have the steady employment which other Canadians across the country enjoy. It is no wonder that native band councils across the country want to resolve this problem with Indian self-government. All Canadians must be very sincere, concerned and aware of this.
The Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development has addressed many issues affecting native people in the last number of weeks and will continue to do so. Sitting down as we do with the officials from the Government and the officials from the band councils across Canada is the proper procedure to resolve the problems. I am looking forward to being able to say, at the end of our four-year term, that we have worked closely and freely and resolved problems which native people have had for years. The prior Government
January 22, 1985

could not say this. It did not sit down with the provincial officials, the federal officials, and the officials of the band councils in order to solve the economic problems which the native people are facing. However, I feel very confident that this Government, my Minister, and officials from coast to coast will be able to do something to resolve the economic problems facing native people. We will be able to help them to have a stronger place in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, on December 4 my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), moved the following motion in the House:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of promoting Indian self-government by:
1.	Announcing support for an affirmative policy of constitutional recognition of aboriginal self-government;
2.	Pursuing actively, a bilateral process of discussion with representatives of first nations on such issues as self-government, natives claims and the elimination of the extinguishment policy; and
3.	Introducing legislation to recognize first nations self-government which should be developed by means of a joint process and utilization of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
I have had the distinct pleasure of serving with the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior on the House of Commons Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I would like to congratulate him for his sincerity and hard work. As Hon. Members of the House probably know, he chaired the special Standing Committee on Indian Self-government, of which I was a part, which resulted in what is commonly known as the Penner report.
That committee travelled across Canada, visited with bands and councils, and heard from native groups. It became clear that as a result of government legislation in the past we have relegated the Indian peoples of this country to a servitude that no sane Canadian would accept in this enlightened day and age.
I agree with the Member for Cochrane-Superior that the Indian people have been mistreated by the very paternalistic approach adopted with respect to their very livelihood. We must remember that it was not too long ago-clearly I can remember it distinctly as a young boy growing up in northern Alberta-when Indian people, if they wanted to leave the reserve, had to go to an Indian agent and ask for permission to do so. First they had to ask permission, then they had to sign out, and finally they had to tell the Indian agent when they would return. It was not so long ago when Indians could not leave the reserve.
Members will recall that Indians were not allowed to vote in any election in Canada. In other words, they were totally disenfranchised from the vote. They could not participate in the democratic process.
Today, Indian people elect their chiefs and have band council members who are elected by the band members on the reserve to administer the law, the band and the band members. This council may pass a resolution to spend funds which they
Indian Self-Government
have generated through resource revenue. However, that resolution must go to Ottawa to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The Minister must then approve that resolution because, through legislation, he is the trustee of all the Indians in Canada. This is clearly unacceptable in this day and age and in this country.
I agree with the Member for Cochrane-Superior that we must address this issue. Let me refer again to some of the problems we face in extinguishing this paternalistic attitude and method of dealing with Indian people. I want to compliment the Member for Cochrane-Superior for his initiative in bringing this Private Member's Bill forward. I want to compliment him for his sincerity and hard work. I believe he is a credit to the House of Commons in everything he has done on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I want that to show clearly on the record, because in the future I think we will look back on his activity in chairing the special committee that travelled across the country and produced the Penner report as a very clear milestone in the inclusion of the Indian people into the mainstream of society. I think we will be very proud of him for having worked for that.
I have one problem with giving unlimited support to his Bill today. I suggest it would be useful to remind not only him but all Members of the House of the recent constitutional developments that have taken place with respect to aboriginal peoples.
In February of 1979, the national native organizations attended the First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution as observers. An agenda item was adopted on "Canada's Native Peoples and the Constitution". In September, 1980, another First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution was held with the national native leaders in attendance as observers.
In late 1980 and early 1981, the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution in Canada held hearings and submitted its final report. It made several specific recommendations, including one on the rights of aboriginal peoples in Canada and on the participation of the aboriginal peoples in constitutional conferences. I believe that a significant milestone was reached at that time.
In 1981, the federal and provincial Governments agreed to the inclusion in the Constitution of a clause recognizing and affirming the existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples. We all know the difficulty we had in inserting that clause by way of provincial and federal negotiations and even in discussions in the House and Committee to ensure that that clause was included in the Constitution of Canada.
In April of 1982, the Constitution Act was proclaimed with several references to aboriginal peoples. For example, Section 25 said:
The guarantee in this Charter of certain rights and freedoms shall not be construed so as to abrogate or derogate from any aboriginal, treaty or other rights or freedoms that pertain to the aboriginal peoples of Canada including:
(A) Any rights or freedoms that have been recognized by the Royal Proclamation of October 7, 1763; and

January 22, 1985
Indian Self-Government
(B) Any rights or freedoms that may be acquired by the aboriginal people in
Canada by way of land claims settlement.
Section 35 says:
(1)	The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal people of
Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
(2)	In this Act. 'aboriginal peoples of Canada' includes the Indian, Inuit and
Metis peoples of Canada.
The requirement for a constitutional conference within a year of proclamation was also included.
In March, 1983, a First Ministers' Conference was held on the rights of aboriginal peoples, with the full participation of aboriginal leaders. It is the first time in the history of Canada that this very sensitive issue was addressed with the full participation of the aboriginal leaders. The outcome of that meeting was a Constitutional Accord to amend the Constitution Act, 1982, and to hold constitutional meetings over three years to identify and define the rights of aboriginal peoples.
The substance of these amendments was to ensure that aboriginal and treaty rights applied equally to male and female persons. I believe that we all know the problems we are facing with that issue. Second, it was to ensure that aboriginal peoples would be involved in formal conferences prior to any amendments to certain sections of the Constitution Acts 18671982. If I may pause for a moment, let me say that the fact that that section alone was agreed to by the leaders of the aboriginal peoples at the constitutional conference precludes us at this time from moving forward with this Private Members' Bill, as much as I and many Members in the House would like to see it moved to committee.
Third, rights acquired through existing and future land claim settlements would be recognized and affirmed in the Constitution in the same way as treaty rights. That is where we face difficulty. We cannot put the cart before the horse.
In March, 1984, a further First Ministers' Conference on the rights of aboriginal peoples was held. No agreement was reached on the four agenda items. The four agenda items, as you will recall, Mr. Speaker, were equality rights: aboriginal title and aboriginal rights; treaties and treaty rights; land and resources; and aboriginal self-government. That bears repeating. No agreement was reached on the four agenda items. You will note, Sir, that the fourth agenda item is aboriginal self-government.
In the spring of 1985, another First Ministers' Conference on aboriginal constitutional matters is scheduled. It is to be followed by another one by April, 1987.
I think clearly, and with great respect to my friend and colleague, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior, this Government is moving and is committed to move in the direction that we want to go, and that is, to bring Indian people of this country along with aboriginal peoples elsewhere, the Inuit, into the mainstream of Canadian society so that they can take their place fully within the total mosaic of our country. They do not like, we do not like, and clearly the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior does not like the situation as it is today. I do not
like the fact that individuals in this country, and some of them first Canadians, grown, capable, industrious men still and women, from a white father in Ottawa, a Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, to live and to do the kind of things that we take for granted every day of our lives. Clearly we have to correct this injustice and clearly the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) is committed to doing that. We on this side of the House, this Government, is committed to doing that and we will do it.
The issues involved in these constitutional negotiations are complex. We all know that. They concern the relationship between aboriginal peoples and the rest of Canadians. The resolution will mark the creation of a new relationship. We have to resolve it and when we do, it will be a new relationship. The relationship under which the Indian people in Canada now function is the kind of relationship that makes them second-class citizens. This has to be changed. We are going to resolve this question. But it will create a whole new relationship with the rest of Canada because of the aboriginal rights, because of the land titles, the land entitlements, the land settlements and the treaty rights. All of these have to be taken into account in this complex issue. In time we will eliminate the terrible bureaucracy that we have known as Indian Affairs and Northern Development or DIAND.
In the area of aboriginal government, the complexity of jurisdictional issues is very obvious. Careful negotiations are needed based on a full and frank expression of aims and needs and the determination to develop a set of intergovernmental relationships that will work well. As we all know, reserves exist in every province in the Northwest Territories and in the Yukon. Because of the complexity of working with another government, some of the reserves work very closely or are very closely aligned with municipalities, such as, for example, the Hobbema Reserve and the Sarcee Reserve in Calgary. The urban sprawl of Calgary is now starting to surround portions of the Sarcee Reserve. We see the same thing happening in Edmonton where the urban sprawl toward the west has started to encompass parts of the reserve. In both cases the band councils of those reserves, with permission, by the way, of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Affairs of previous governments, have developed subdivisions. We find the same thing in Vancouver and Victoria. The jurisdictional issues are obviously very complex.
The Canadian political tradition is based on interdependence and co-operation among several orders of government. How then are we to fit them in when Indian self-government becomes a reality? How do we fit them in with what we have existing today? Clearly our tradition is based on co-operation. We have gone through a period now of 10 to 15 years or so when there was not too much co-operation between the provincial and federal governments. This new Government is changing that. The signs and the results of that change are showing up right across the country. Because of the powers and functioning stemming from the Constitution, aboriginal government will have to fit into and be part of this political tradition.
January 22, 1985

I am sorry that I cannot support sending this Private Member's Bill from a colleague whom I admire very much. We will all be proud that he was a Member sitting in this House of Commons when we were here, because we will look back on the work he has done on behalf of aboriginal native people with sincere and distinct pride. I see that my time has elapsed, Mr. Speaker. I am sorry that I must sit down because I had a few more comments to make. Because of the complexity of the issue, we will be addressing it again, and I know the Hon. Member will play a very significant role in any decision that comes out of this House of Commons, or indeed out of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to speak on this Bill this afternoon and to outline some very serious concerns that I have on the matter of native self-government.
I think everyone in this House believes that the native people in Canada do have the right to self-government. It is a right that must be re-established. It was never sold, it was never surrendered, and this Government must take responsibility for recognizing and returning that right to the native people as quickly as possible.
If there is no doubt on that particular issue, I would like to outline briefly the activities of an Indian band in my riding. I am speaking of the Sechelts. The Sechelts have been in the forefront of a campaign to make the relationship with the Government of Canada and the native people in Canada more human. They have taken a very positive, dynamic and energetic stance on this question, particularly the question of native self-government. They have expended a great deal of their resources. It has been a major priority of Chief Stan Dixon, with the Sechelt Band council and people. The expenditure of time and resources on this project has been enormous.
I should like to refer to the basic approach of the Sechelt people. As a result of their experience, their administration in the past, their development, execution and planning of projects, the Sechelt people have developed their band resources to the maximum under the present restrictive nature of the Indian Act. They have taken advantage of all discretionary options that are available. They are still hampered. The quality of life and the potential of the Sechelt people are still hampered by the colonial and fraternalistic legislation which the Government of Canada imposes on all Indian people.
In the face of that difficulty, the Sechelt people, the Sechelt Band Council and Chief Stan Dixon produced a suggestion for the Government of Canada. It was produced a number of years ago and was called the Sechelt Indian Band Act. Their proposal was that the House of Commons should consider this legislation. It was simply an enabling piece of legislation which recognized the right of these people to develop a constitution appropriate to their community. Also it would allow them to pursue activities, as other Canadians under their forms of
Indian Self-Government
self-government could do, to improve the quality of life of the citizens of that community.
Unfortunately, as time went by they ran up against government obstacles. I will go back a step and describe what happened. They had approached the district level of Indian Affairs and had received support and assistance for their concept. At the regional level in the western region of Indian Affairs, they obtained financial support and assistance in developing a concept for a Sechelt Indian Band Act and their constitution. They obtained support from the regional district and then came to Ottawa where the concept was supported once again. They approached Members of the House and obtained support for the concept. They approached the last Minister who gave them support. He said that he would be prepared to introduce legislation which would allow the Sechelt Indian people to move forward with their particular form of self-government.
Unfortunately, it became tangled in the race for the leadership of the Liberal Party. It was delayed and delayed until the end of the last Parliament. Instead of becoming discouraged, the Sechelt Indian people again approached all Parties in the House of Commons. They approached the Department of Indian Affairs. Once again they are ready to place before this institution a piece of self-government legislation which would enable their band to develop a constitution appropriate for their community.
It is my understanding that the Government and the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crom-bie) are familiar with this particular piece of legislation, and that they have accepted it as a pilot project to be used in the development of the concept of native self-government and will be introducing it in the House before the end of January. It is my hope that the Minister will be introducing that legislation. He can be certain of the support of the New Democratic Party in expediting that piece of legislation through the House of Commons to meet the needs of the Sechelt people.
The Sechelt Indian Band produced a piece of legislation which I think is appropriate for a pilot project to begin the process of native self-government. Parliament must do something quickly and effectively to recognize and restore that right to native people in the country. In the development and application of this project, the Sechelt people could act as a model which may or may not be appropriate for other bands. Certainly it would be a positive move. If the Minister acts quickly to expedite that piece of legislation through the House, it would allow the Sechelt people to put their construction in place, begin to develop the process of self-government, to remove themselves from the restrictive nature of the Indian Act, and to begin the process of setting up a pilot project with this particular piece of legislation.
Certainly there is a financial side to the situation. It is recognized that the Government of Canada has a financial responsibility to native communities. The Sechelt Indian Band and its people have put forward a proposal to expedite and make more meaningful the financial relationship between the Government of Canada and those people, as well as others who

January 22, 1985
Indian Self-Government
would organize their self-government process. This financial commitment must be recognized. Certainly in passing the membership legislation in the last Parliament to remedy the problems under Section 12(l)(b), we ran squarely into the question of whether it is correct to restore membership to a native community over the heads of the people in that community. We failed to recognize the critical need to provide financial resources to those communities to establish those new members in a fair and equitable way. We must deal with that.
It is my hope that the Government will live up to its commitments to the Sechelt Indian people. I hope it introduces the legislation before the end of January so that the House can deal with it in a quick and expeditious manner and possibly implement one of the first solid endeavours in native self-government in Canada. It would be a credit to the Government and to the Sechelt people who have worked so long and hard on this particular matter.
I should like to read into the record a couple of quotations of Chief Stan Dixon. The first one was reported as follows:
The Sechelt band has steadily maintained its interest in being "masters of our own destiny." They feel implementation of proposed legislation would leave them free of the Department of Indian Affairs, and in control, but still enjoying the aboriginal and constitutional rights of indigenous people.
Another quotation read:
Our proposal is simply an interim step which will permit us and others who wish to free themselves from the rigidity of the current Indian Act, to do so with a charter developed at the band level.
What could be simpler? What basic right could be more easily recognized than this particular situation?
It goes without saying that many of the aspects with which the House has failed to deal are extremely important. However, none is more important than the aspect of native self-government. It is a right of the Indian people. That right has to be recognized. It was never extinguished. It was never bought. It was never surrendered. It must be restored.
In the self-government issue there are a number of very important matters. One is education. The right of Indian people to develop a quality of life which is normal and expected in the country has been hampered ever since the present Government of Canada took office. There are enormous drop-out rates in native communities. I was astounded when I visited a number of those communities to learn that drop-out rates are still enormous. The average level of education of a native child in my area reaches up to about grade 10. Certainly there are many communities which receive even less than that. The federal Government has cut back on its funding for native education. Indian children do not have anywhere near the same opportunities as those enjoyed by any other children in Canada. That is a complete disgrace. That disgrace on the country could be eliminated by a decision of Parliament to accept its responsibility to provide Indian children in Canada enough in the way of financial resources to provide education. The Government, in its narrow and tight policy, is failing to meet the educational needs of Indian children. It is destroying the quality of life by that single act, as well as the quality of opportunity for native children.
I spoke with a chief on the central coast of British Columbia who indicated that their problems were financial. He also indicated that they had transportation problems, as well as problems in terms of establishing their rights as a people in the country. He indicated that above all else one of their greatest problems was the problem of human resources. They cannot educate their children because the Government will simply not give them the funds which it gives to other children in the country. Even with the funds which they are given under the master tuition agreement, for example to the Province of British Columbia, they have no guarantees that they are expended in the best interests of Indian children.
This Government must give control over education dollars to those who would direct them most appropriately. The native people of British Columbia, and indeed of all Canada, must have some say in exercising the expenditure of those dollars. One small school district represents tens of thousands of dollars each year. Although the particular school district collects those dollars each year, it does not do what is required for native people. It does not happen and will not hapen until we give control over those federal education dollars to the native people, particularly in the case of British Columbia. It is widely believed that the Province of B.C. is expending those funds in an inappropriate manner. They do not recognize in an effective way the rights of native people to an education.
There are serious questions about the use of those funds. I believe it would be appropriated for the Minister of Indian Affairs to launch an investigation into the expenditures by the Province of British Columbia which we provide under the master tuition agreement and other federal programs. It is widely believed that those funds are not being expended according to the wishes and the programs of the federal Government.
The recognition of those students and the provision of funds to enable them to obtain a post-secondary education or technical training is not being done by the federal Government. It is my understanding that it cut off those funds. It is my belief and the belief of many other people in this House that the federal Government has a responsibility to native children to ensure that they obtain a proper education, take their rightful place and establish a quality of life. It is time we restored that funding to ensure that native children have an opportunity to attend university, technical schools, vocational schools and community colleges. We must provide the resource base to those bands in order that they can begin to develop. This is critically important. It is a serious neglect of our responsibilities in terms of the Government of Canada not to provide those funds.
There is another matter that is important in the issue of self-government. In establishing the needs of native communities through some kind of access, it is important to have a financially stable economic base. This Government must push harder. It must make a solid commitment to resolve questions of the aboriginal land claim. The Province of British Columbia
January 22, 1985

is completely negligent and completely irresponsible in resolving this matter, in recognizing the rights of aboriginal people to the area which they inhabit and the resource base they used in former times. Much of this has been usurped and used for the benefit of communities other than native communities.
One example brought to me time and again is that of the small reserves that were given in the Province of British Columbia. They were not given access to minerals, fossil fuels and timber as was done in other areas of Canada because of a large land base. They were not given access to those resources even though they use they in them in their day to day lives. The reason for the small land reserve base in British Columbia was that those communities were so heavily dependent on fishing. That reason was stated time and again. Native people in British Columbia have been removed from the fishing resource to a large degree. The reserves are too small to handle the people who live there. That is one reason why so many people live in other communities. Often 50, 60 or 70 per cent of the people cannot live on the these small reserves with the inadequate funding.
It will be clearly established that native people have the right and have a claim against territories and resources they previously used. If we provide access to the resource base, the land, fish, timber and mineral resources used in previous times in areas over which those bands had jurisdiction, it would be a way by which those bands could establish some financial and economic security. Unless we give them access, they are not going to be able to re-establish any wealth or financial security.
This Government must move quickly, in advance of the settlement of the land claims, to provide, where possible, access to resource where the native communities have the resources and are in need of assistance. We had an example in the House the day when the Conservatives raised the matter of forestry and criticized the forestry policy in Canada. There was agreement among all Parties to press development of a forestry program within the Department of Indian Affairs for native people. As yet, nothing serious has happened on that. I challenge members of the present Government who stood on the floor of this House in opposition and made a commitment to do something to provide now access to forestry and to do so in a very thorough manner. That is one example.
Access to the fishing resource must come about. Where land is available, it has to be provided. In short, we must begin the process in advance of convincing our colleagues in British Columbia, who are almost neanderthal on this concept, that something can be done to provide a base of wealth for native people.
I see my time is up, Mr. Speaker. Thank you for the opportunity to express my thoughts.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. Oberle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Mines)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Mines)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take pleasure in contributing briefly to the debate this afternoon. As Hon. Members will know, along with the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), I shared the responsibility for developing a
Indian Self-Government
blueprint for the future, as the Penner report has come to be known, in terms of the future relationship between the Government of Canada, the other partners in Confederation and our native people.
I naturally applaud my hon. friend for bringing this motion before the House. However, I must tell him immediately that there is a fundamental flaw in his motion. As all of us know, if this motion were to pass the House this afternoon, it would be referred to committee.
The flaw that I see in the Hon. Member's motion is that the committee has already dealt with this matter. The Hon. Member and myself, together with several of our colleagues, worked one and a half years and travelled throughout the country in developing a self-government report with 58 very distinct recommendations incorporated in it. That report was tabled in the House. The committee has spoken. It has done its work. As I said, the committee produced a blueprint for the future and, indeed, that is what it is.
Naturally the Hon. Member has to use this opportunity to highlight the affair throughout the country again. However, absolutely no purpose would be served if this matter were once again referred to committee.
I have little problem with the Hon. Member's motion which proposes to affirm the concept of aboriginal rights. As my colleague from Athabasca (Mr. Shields) stated, that is no longer a question. That concept is entrenched in our Constitution in a manner which can no longer abrogate from the distinct rights which native people have in this country, dating back to the Royal Proclamation of 1763.
There is no need to reaffirm this concept. It is done. The question we have to come to grips with now is, what does the concept of aboriginal rights mean? It means different things to different people. There are 258 bands or so-called nations throughout this country. If you meet with all of them, as we attempted to do, you discover that the concept of aboriginal rights and title means something different to all 258 of them. However, there are certain recurring themes, trends and principles that the committee immediately discovered as being consistent throughout. We found, for instance, that to all people, the concept of aboriginal rights means the right to self-determination and the right to self-government. That became very apparent and there was no dissension. It is proper for the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior who was the chairman of that special committee to remind the House of the fact that there is, first, the recognition of the concept of aboriginal rights and, second, that it means the right to self-determination and the right to self-government.
Regarding the form, nature and responsibilities of these self-government structures, the committee report is mute for a very good reason. Again, throughout our deliberations in all parts of the country with different tribal associations, bands and nations, we discovered that everyone had a different idea of the kind of structure they would like to see and which would serve best their heritage, traditions, culture and religion. It

January 22, 1985
Indian Self-Government
would have been wrong for us, the committee, and indeed it would be wrong for the Government to impose a structure of government that would not be suitable to these legitimate aspirations of our native people. For that reason, the committee did not lay out any distinct form of government but laid out a general framework of a self-government structure which would then be left to negotiations between Indian nations and a special representative of the federal Government to define.
Much of the definition of self-government deals with the responsibility that these native leaders would have to assume and with how they would be accountable to the people they lead and govern. Should they be accountable in the same way as we are responsible to our constituents or, as natives, and because of their distinct and traditional form of governing themselves, do they have a better way? That must be discussed. I would venture to guess that there would be a number of different ways in which native people could prove to us that they are and can be responsible to their constituents.
Previous speakers have mentioned the economic foundation upon which these governments will be built. Membership is a critical issue. Another subcommittee dealt with the question of membership and the discrimination section of the Indian Act which has a bearing on this critical question.
I would like to call these forms of governments distinct forms of governments because they will not be municipal or provincial governments but will be distinct forms that will operate within the framework of Confederation. This is another item that the committee established. It is the committee's wish and determination that Indian people join Confederation in a distinct and different way.
We will have to establish how these new governments will relate first to other governments, municipal, provincial and federal, and how they will relate to other native people including the Metis, the so-called non-status people who call themselves the forgotten people, and the Inuit who are not embraced within this discussion. All of these things must be discussed.
It is unfortunate that the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior is not present today. I would not like to see the new Government proceed with the same indecent haste with which the former Government proceeded five minutes to 12 before the election. It brought in a Bill giving all things to all people without consultation or dialogue. The Bill was designed for no other purpose than to get it past the election and earn it the affection of the Indian people who had been so thoroughly disappointed by the former Government. I would not* support that kind of initiative and I do not think that the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior would either.
I believe that our dialogue with native people should proceed in the same way as our dialogue is proceeding with the provincial Governments under a new form of co-operative federalism because, after all, we do intend to incorporate and embrace Indian governments in a new scheme of co-operative federalism. We would want very much to know from the native people how they would want us to proceed.
I can tell the House, the country and you, Mr. Speaker, that it is the intention of the new Government to proceed expeditiously, with care, fairness and sensitivity but with firmness as well toward the development of a better relationship with our native people. We will proceed in a manner that is more consistent with the Canadian tradition and is fair, just and designed to repair some of the injustices of the past.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy indeed to take the first opportunity in the House afforded to me to speak on a subject other than a statement or a question. The reason I wish to speak on the issue of Indian self-government is that I myself am one of the people. Even though I am not a member of one of the Indian tribes, I am of the Inuit people who were commonly known in the world as Eskimos. However, I do not consider myself to be an Eskimo. That is a term which is offensive to the Inuit.
I was one of the past directors of land claims and one of the chief negotiators of our organization from the Northwest Territories for the past four years. We have been negotiating with the Government of Canada since 1974-75. When the Inuit discuss self-government, they want to include everything which governments normally include. However, over the years, we have found, as the Parliamentary Secretary mentioned, that there were so many concepts that it is difficult to come to terms with this unless one goes through a long process.
One of the processes which the Inuit of Nunavut have attempted to use is the political route. We have attempted to use the Territorial Government route by calling for the division of the Northwest Territories. I am happy to inform other Members of the House that a little over one week ago, the groups from the eastern Arctic and the western Arctic had come to some terms over the issue of boundaries. I am sure that over the next few weeks and months, more issues will arise and be clarified.
I would want to see the Government of Canada deal first with the large issue of the division of the Northwest Territories, an issue which has been a consistent theme of the Inuit people in my riding. It is not a radical concept, but a concept which follows the traditional forms of debate in terms of the formation of public governments.
