subtopic: AGRICULTURE-EFFECT OF BANK INTEREST RATES ON FARMERS. (B) GOVERNMENT ACTION
AGRICULTURE-EFFECT OF BANK INTEREST RATES ON FARMERS. (B) GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 20, 1984, I asked the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) if the Government intended to keep its promise to write down all outstanding farm loans to present-day interest rates. The Minister waffled a bit and gave a lot of verbiage, but did not indicate much action in his response.
There is a very serious crisis facing thousands and thousands of young farmers in Canada today. A recent study by the Farm Credit Corporation indicated that 39,000 farmers in Canada are in serious financial difficulty. The criterion for judging that difficulty is that those farmers are paying more than 40 per cent of their gross revenues to cover payments on their properties. The second criterion is that the actual ownership of the farm operations, the equity, is less than 15 per cent. The third criteron is that the farmers are borrowing more than they are investing in capital on the farm. When we apply those criteria we find that each of the 39,000 farmers is subject to one or more of those criteria. It is a very serious situation.
The personal tragedy of all this is that most of the 39,000 farmers are young. They are our most innovative farmers, the farmers who have applied new technology. In fact, they produce half of all the produce produced in Canada each year.
The Government to this point has not taken any decisive or effective steps to help the vast majority of those farmers who are facing bankruptcy or total collapse. The Minister of Agriculture brought in a modest program a few weeks ago which would reduce interest rates from 14 per cent or 15 per cent down to 12.75 per cent for a specific period, during 1981 and 1982. However, we must look at that measure in light of the recommendation which was made by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, the National Farmers Union and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that certain commodity groups require interest rates in the area of about 8 per cent.
An announcement was made last week by the Minister of Agriculture for Manitoba that legislation would be brought in to block all farm foreclosures unless the Government and the bank reduced interest rates to 8 per cent. The disturbing part of this is that the Minister of Agriculture for Saskatchewan has already done that. If the Minister of Agriculture for Manitoba does the same thing, I believe there will be chaos in the farm financing situation. Fist, credit will dry up from the bankers in Manitoba to the farm producers. That credit would enable farm producers to put in their crops next spring. Bankers in other provinces, in anticipation of the action of those provinces, will impose a debt moratorium and will continue with foreclosures. There are currently thousands of
Adjournment Debate
cases in which foreclosure action could be taken. It will end up in chaos in farm financing.
If we compare what this Government has done, essentially nothing, to forestall these bankruptcies, with what the Farmers Home Administration is doing in the United States, we will see that they have a program which sets aside one-quarter of the farm debt for up to five years. We will also see that they have already processed something like 477 applications in the first month of that program. They anticipate 150,000 applications and are ready to look after them. They have already lowered the rates on 8,000 approved loans from 11 per cent or 12 per cent to 7 per cent or 5 per cent. What we have in the United States is a very effective program to set aside a portion of the debt to forestall these bankruptcies and stop the kind of chaos we see developing among these 39,000 farmers affected by low commodity prices, decreasing land value and high interest rates. I hope the Parliamentary Secretary will be able to respond in a positive way this evening.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-EFFECT OF BANK INTEREST RATES ON FARMERS. (B) GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture and the Government of Canada, I am pleased with this opportunity to answer the question put by the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster). The question raised on November 20 referred to high interest rates and what the Government was doing to help farmers beset by financial problems. Unfortunately, the Hon. Member for Algoma does not seem to recall, although I agree farmers are faced with a difficult and in some cases precarious situation with interest rates of 16 and 17 per cent, that our Government was not in power when those rates were in effect.
Last week in Quebec City, the Minister of Agriculture announced that we were fulfilling yet another of our election promises. We had promised farmers we would make available immediately the necessary funds to help them refinance their loans at current-day interest rates.
I should explain that we have received many requests for assistance from farmers with long-term loans locked in at high interest rates with the Farm Credit Corporation. They took out loans when interest rates, and I think you will remember that, had reached their maximum and the FCC refused to let them set the due date. As a result, they were committed to repayment of their loans over periods of as much as 20 or 30 years at rates varying from 14 to 16 % per cent. Most of them are unable to refinance their loans at a lower rate with a commercial financial institution or through small business bonds.
That is why the Minister announced that all farmers who took out loans with the Farm Credit Corporation between April 1, 1981 and December 8, 1982 will be able to write down their rates to 123/4 per cent as of January 1, 1985. This decision will affect 5,600 FCC customers, who have already been

January 22, 1985
Adjournment Debate
informed of the details and the procedure to be followed. All this will be retroactive to January 1, and represents an annual saving of $16 million over the next five years for this group of borrowers. The announcement may have an impact on a number of foreclosures ordered by the FCC. The temporary suspension expired on January 16, but all borrowers whose assets have been seized may now have their case reviewed by an independent appeal board. Measures to that effect were also announced last December. Furthermore, these borrowers can have their case reassessed and if possible have their interest rates written down to a lower rate.
Mr. Speaker, yesterday we had some more positive announcements with respect to farm credit. The FCC has lowered its interest rates as of January 21. Rates have been reduced from 13 Vi to 12% and finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that it would of course be nice, as my colleague from Algoma suggested, to reduce interest rates to 6 and 8 per cent, but I think everyone will agree that we have already made some headway if we consider the rates of 16 and 17 per cent we had a few years ago under the previous government.

subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-UNLICENSED CABLE TELEVISION OPERATORS-PROSECUTION QUERY (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-UNLICENSED CABLE TELEVISION OPERATORS-PROSECUTION QUERY (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 3, 1984 I called on the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) to bring justice to the area of the cable TV operators, licensed and unlicensed, in this country. Instead of dealing with the problem an incredible confusion in the industry has been created. This confusion is risking the destruction of the Canadian broadcasting system. It is damaging the rights of licensed cable operators and is leading to very serious financial losses to them.
I rise today to state the case in somewhat more detail. I understand there are two Parliamentary Secretaries here to answer this, but I think it would take a fleet of Parliamentary Secretaries. I do not think there is a good answer to it.
There are now two classes of operators in the cable TV field in the country. There is one class which went to the CRTC and was awarded licenses. They are Canadian owned and carry Canadian content. They are restricted in the amount of American programming they can carry. They pay the Americans for the programming that they use and, in addition, pay a 6 per cent tax to a special fund to create financing for Canadian content and programming in our country. They operate in this country.
At the same time, within their territory, there are operators who did not go to the CRTC, or if they went were turned down and not given a licenses. They established anyway. They are not necessarily Canadian owned and definitely do not carry Canadian content. They pick up American signals from the air without paying the Americans anything for them. They can pick up whatever they like, even channels which are not
available to the licensed broadcasters, such as the Disney channel, some channels that carry spicey movies, HBO and Cinemax. They can pick up a whole bunch of lines which are there but which the licensed operators cannot carry. They offer all of these at lower cost to the same people who are now being served by the licensed TV operators. As well, that they do not pay the 6 per cent tax to this fund for Canadian programming.
The former Government began to prosecute the unlicensed cable operators in order to protect the rights which had been awarded to the licensed operators. For example, in Salmon Arm, British Columbia I understand that the two operations are right across the street from each other. One person holds a license and is meeting all of the conditions that I just described, and his competitor across the street is not meeting any of them, and was going to be prosecuted by the former Government when the present Attorney General of Canada directed that these prosecutions be stayed.
I think the reason that they were stayed was because of the last election campaign. I understand there are over 500 unlicensed cable operators in the Prairie provinces alone operating against the licensed operators without licenses or restrictions of any kind. Tory candidates must have gone to them and told them to keep going, that they would bail them out if they won the election. They won the election. The unlicensed operators have been bailed out. When they heard that the prosecutions had been stayed they went ahead and announced that they had won a great victory. They increased their numbers of subscribers, damaging those who were carrying Canadian content, paying the tax and paying the Americans for the channels they were taking from the United States. A great victory was won by the others.
This is a terrible mess. The broadcasting system is suffering as is Canadian content. The property rights of individuals who applied for licenses and got them are suffering. The Government is doing nothing about it.

speakeroldname: Mr. Chris Speyer (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE-UNLICENSED CABLE TELEVISION OPERATORS-PROSECUTION QUERY (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in fulfilling the role of chief law officer of the Crown, the Attorney General of Canada is called upon to exercise the judgment and discretion which he feels is in the public interest. He is guided by certain parliamentary, legal and constitutional principles and may look to a rich heritage in the tradition of the holders of that high office both in Canada and Great Britain.
In arriving at a decision whether to proceed with a prosecution, the Attorney General is entitled to seek information and advice from others. That is not to say that he is directed in the course of his discretion by his colleagues or by Parliament itself. Nor is it suggested that the Attorney General is not accountable to Parliament for his decision, which he obviously is.
Anyone who properly understands the position and function of the Attorney General will be able to appreciate that the
January 22, 1985

recent decision with regard to the Broadcasting Act cases was undertaken properly in accordance with our best traditions of both principle and traditions.
As the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Crosbie) has already stated, his decision was based on considerations of public order and policy. He ascertained, with reference to one of his colleagues in Government, that an imminent change in the Government's Broadcasting policy was being planned. As everyone knowledgeable on the subject is already aware, it has been increasingly difficult in recent years to harmonize the law with the realities of the evolving technology as it relates to the distribution of television programming signals to rural and remote communities in Canada.
In these circumstances, with a handful of cases about to be tried in the criminal courts and reconsideration of regulatory policy about to be undertaken, the Attorney General came to the conclusion that the prosecution of those cases should be stayed, pending reconsideration which might well affect some or all of these cases which, by that time, would have been tried. That is the reason for the position that was taken by the Attorney General.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING-AWARDING OF CONTRACT. (B) MEASURES TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT
GOVERNMENT ADVERTISING-AWARDING OF CONTRACT. (B) MEASURES TAKEN BY GOVERNMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the federal election campaign, one of the major promises of the Progressive Conservative Party was to clean up the mess of patronage left by the Liberals during their last years of office.
Last July, in one of the few acts in office, the Turner Government awarded a 21-month contract as Agency of Record to a consortium of four advertising agencies known as Canadian Media Corp., with strong ties to the Liberal Party. When that deal became known, the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) was quite forthright about it; a deal which was carried out in top secret without any bids being called. He said the Turner Government was "dipping low into the Liberal porkbarrel".

Mr. Speaker, I asked for this adjournment debate because I find it impossible to distinguish the contract awarded in January to Media Canada as the federal Government's Agency of Record from what the Liberals have done before, except that now the Progressive Conservatives and not the Liberals are going to benefit. Hon. Members are aware of the comments made by Mr. Roger Nantel of Montreal, one of the directors of Media Canada, when the contract was made public. He was the Progressive Conservative Party's chief of communications in Quebec City during the election campaign. His comments implied that the company had made some kind of agreement with the Progressive Conservative Party as one of the conditions of the contract with the Government of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, these statements are now being investigated by the RCMP. It is quite clear that. . . regardless of the competence of Mr. Nantel and his partner, Mr. Simpson, they were
Adjournment Debate
awarded the contract mainly because they are Progressive Conservatives who in the past have worked for the Progressive Conservative Party and who are continuing to work for the Progressive Conservative Party.

When I raised this question yesterday, I suggested that the Government's rules for contracting for services were being grossly violated by the decision to negotiate a contract with one supplier of media buying services with no effort to call tenders or look at the capabilities of other suppliers. The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre) suggested that the advertising business is not amenable to tender. His office told my office that a contract like this one is exempt from tendering under Treasury Board regulations.
I have checked those regulations and the answer is, that is just not so. The Government's own regulations about service contracts indicate otherwise. Paragraph 3.1 of the contract with Media Canada states specifically that "This is intended to be a service contract within the meaning of the Government Contracts Regulations (PC 1975-2042)". These were the regulations that I quoted from in the House on Monday. Section 8 of these regulations is explicit in calling for a contracting authority to invite tenders, "before any contract is entered into" except for emergencies, for small contracts where it would not be in the public interest or where only one person or company is capable of performing the contract.
The amendments made to this government contract regulations since 1975 contain no exemptions for advertising. Nor was that step taken by the Clark Government when it established the Agency of Record system. A change in the Agency of Record is not an emergency. It is a substantial contract. It is hard to see how it would be against the public interest to invite tenders. Also more than one company is capable of fulfilling a contract.

Mr. Speaker, it is quite clear that part of the problems facing us today are due to abuse of the tender system for service contracts with the Government. In some newspaper articles it was said that 85 per cent of service contracts, representing a value of over $2 billion annually, are awarded without tender.

However, if the new Government were permitted to change it, it would be seeking to clean out the system left by the Liberals, not perpetuating it.
Mr. Andre says that contracts like this are not amenable to Canada. Yet it is common in the advertising business for agencies to compete for contracts, not on the basis of price, but on the basis of the quality of their presentation. Moreover, Mr. Andre-

Mr. Speaker, first let me make it clear that no contract for $1.8 million has been awarded as the Hon. Member suggested in his question the other day. The company headed by Messrs. Nantel and Simpson, to which my hon. colleague refers, is in receipt of a contract worth $375,000.

This Government has saved $18,000 a month in terms of those advertising contracts. If the comparison were to be drawn between this contract and similar awards made under the previous regime, it would be seen that on a monthly basis this
Government has saved the taxpayer

I repeat-$18,000 a month. The new deal that was entered into was negotiated bearing in mind this Government's commitment to working in the interests of the Canadian taxpayer wherever possible. Let us make one thing clear.
Traditionally the appointment of the Agency of Record was never one that was subjected to the competitive process. Indeed, I should point out that the principle of the Agency of Record, introduced by Peter Simpson in 1979, has resulted in substantial savings to the Government. In fact, by using the Agency of Record, the Government has achieved savings of some $3.6 million since 1981.
I have already said that the Government is committed to acting in the interests of both this country and its taxpayers. The objective of this Government is not patronage, not costly prestige, but solid savings so that our national economy can gain much needed momentum.
The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Andre) has already stated in this House that the business of advertising does not lend itself readily to the competitive process. It should be possible to select the most appropriate organization able to provide its client the services that are required for each specific program or project.
